speechtext:
Mr. MARK C. SENN (Haldimand) presented the fourth report of the select standing committee on agriculture and colonization as follows:	'
At the first meeting of the committee held for this purpose, the Hon. Mr. Weir, Minister of Agriculture, made a brief statement outlining his reasons for making the reference, and the course which he thought the committee should follow:
Your committee has called and examined the following named witnesses:-
W. A. Brown, chief of poultry division, Department of Agriculture.
A. W. Ault, egg and poultry division. Department of Agriculture.
W. L. Brown, member of the firm of William Brown Company, cattle importers, Manchester, England.
A. A. MacMillan, chief of sheep and swine division, Department of Agriculture.
S. E. Todd, Secretary of the Industrial and Development Council of Canada Meat Packers.
W. A. Amos, President, United Farmers' Cooperative Ltd.
W. West, egg dealer, Almonte, Ontario.
Jas. C. Richardson, grain merchant, member of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange.
Sydney T. Smith, representative of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. '
Andrew Cairns, representative of Canadian Wheat Pool.
The agricultural products more particularly studied included eggs, pork and pork products, beef and beef cattle, and exportable wheat.
With respect to the production, grading and marketing of eggs, your committee was fully informed by witnesses, W. A. Brown, chief of the poultry division and A. W. Ault, both of the Department of Agriculture, and also heard representations by witness W. West, an egg dealer of Almonte, Ontario.
Departmental regulations governing the grading and marketing of eggs -were carefully and fully examined and explained and the activities of the department officials charged with the enforcement thereof, fully gone into. The committee was informed that the federal government jurisdiction in this respect extended only to interprovincial and import and export trade, and that enabling legislation by the several provinces was necessary to the enforcement of such regulations. The position in this respect is that all of the provinces with the exception of Ontario and Quebec, have passed the necessary legislation to make enforceable the regulations promulgated in 1929. The regulations of 1924 are enforceable in the province of Ontario.
Notwithstanding the absence of authority to enforce the regulations of 1929 in Ontario and Quebec, the department officials find that voluntary cooperation by the trade is increasing from year to year.
Your committee is of the opinion that the principle of marketing poultry and eggs on a graded standard is in the interest of the producer, dealer and consumer, and recommends that every effort be made to insure the least possible difficulty in the handling, grading and

Agriculture Committee Report
marketing of poultry products, and to guarantee the greatest possible return to the producer.
The committee was fortunate in having appear before it, Mr. W. L. Brown, a member of the firm of William Brown & Company, Manchester, England, buyers and importers of beef cattle. _Mr. Brown gave a comprehensive statement of the conditions obtaining in the British market, the competition met and to be met by Canadian cattle, and the desirable class of beef cattle required by the British market. Mr. W. A. Amos, President of the United Farmers' Co-operative, Limited, also gave the committee valuable evidence.
The committee is of opinion that an export trade of increasing volume and value in beef cattle is open to this country dependent on the following conditions:-
(a)	Careful breeding, feeding, selection and conditioning of Canadian cattle.
(b)	Adequate shipping space.
(c)	Reasonable transportation rates, both rail and ocean.
(d)	A continuous and sufficient volume of available shipments the year round irrespective of the fluctuations in the market prices.
The committee therefore recommends that the foregoing conditions should be carefully and fully studied by the government with a view to bringing the same into effect.
Your committee went very thoroughly into the subject of hog production, breeding and marketing in relation to the requirements of the domestic market and the export trade.
Mr. A. A. MacMillan, chief of the swine division of the Department of Agriculture, Mr. Todd of the Canadian Packers and Mr. W. A. Amos, President of the United Farmers' Cooperative, Limited, gave valuable evidence in this respect. The committee held an informal meeting at the plant of Canada Packers, Limited, where, under the direction of Mr. Todd, a demonstration of the grading of live hogs was given, and an exhibit of dressed hogs of the several government grades was shown. Also cuts were made showing Wiltshire sides and the domestic cuts. This demonstration was exceedingly instructive.
The government hog regulations, their intent, effect, and application were fully considered and your committee is of the opinion that: Every effort should be made to improve the present system of grading so as to secure the least possible difficulty in the handling and marketing of same, and to insure the greatest possible return to the producer. In this regard we commend the Department of Agriculture in the experiments which are being conducted by way of comparison of grading on the hoof and grading on the rail.
Your committee has also given consideration to the wheat situation.
Representatives of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange and of the Canadian wheat pools, upon invitation, appeared before the committee and expressed their views of the situation. Suggestions for the marketing of the carry-over wheat and of the export crop of 1931 were advanced. Reference was made to the negotiations now proceeding between the pools, the banks, the western provinces and the federal government.
In view of the evidence given before the committee, it is recommended that the government take whatever steps it may deem necessary to prevent a drastic decline in the price
paid to producers of wheat, especially during the fall months when the bulk of the crop is being marketed.
Your committee commends the experimental work carried on by the Department of Agriculture and particularly urges the continuance of efforts to inquire into and to disseminate information to the farmers in respect to:
(a)	The causes of and remedy for soil drifting. especially on the open prairies;
(b)	Precautions to take in seeding down to grass or clover, or the planting of trees and hedges or other means;
(e)	Any other matter pertaining to or allied with the live stock and live stock products industry in any part of Canada.
The important question of how to get the producer the maximum returns for his produce and the relation of the spread between producer and consumer was given careful study by your committee.
It is recommended that the Department of Agriculture should take whatever steps be deemed most efficient to obtain all available information on factors determining the spread between what the producer receives and what the_ consumer pays.
Your committee submits herewith its minutes of proceedings and evidence as an appendix to this report, and recommends that the said minutes and report be printed as an appendix to the Journals of the House.

speechtext: Do it now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext:
The adoption of this
resolution lays the foundation for the introduction of a bfll for the purpose of vesting in the governor general in council during the recess of parliament and until the end of the fiscal year full power to redress so far as it is possible the conditions of unemployment and distress now prevalent in certain sections of the Dominion. Comprehensive measures of relief cannot under the circumstances be undertaken without the expenditure of large sums of money. The expenditure of moneys not directly derived from current revenues should not be made without the clearest justification, and the justification which we plead, and which we claim is sufficient. in the interest of Canada as a whole.
The economic situation is apparent to parliament and to the public. It is not the intention of the government to minimize the gravity of it, nor is it its desire politically to profit by it. After the most searching inquiry the full facts of the situation are before us. The causes underlying the present state of affairs may be analyzed at another time when the electors are again asked to determine the form of economic structure most likely to sustain this country in hard times and to prosper it in better times. During the campaign which ended a year ago yesterday I repeatedly said that many of the causes contributing to the disruption of business in other lands had no place in Canada. I said so then; I say so now, and I maintain that this country has a right to expect that however good conditions may be elsewhere, they should be better here. This government
427b

Farm and Unemployment Relief
is not content with the knowledge that others are suffering more than we. What alone concerns us is that many of our people are now in want, and unless extraordinary measures are taken many more will know hardship and privation in the coming months of winter. Knowing this it becomes our solemn duty to aid them. In the short session of parliament last September and in the one now drawing to a close this government did all within its power to strengthen our economic structure and to repulse the wave of worldwide economic depression which was then upon us. I believe that we may fairly claim to have done much. The facts support this belief, but the maximum benefits of any measure of reform cannot be realized in a day or in a year. But, indeed, a short time more I think will prove conclusively that we were right. Of that I am convinced, and of this as well, that the policy of this government will put Canada in the van of the world's recovery.
I have said that I do not wish to make political capital of the present situation. I do not claim that even had this country for many years known the ideal in economic policies we would have been unaffected by the present world conditions, immeasurably aggravated as they have been Recently by the partial failure of t'he wheat crop in the west. In that regard if hon. members of this house will study the immigration returns for the fifteen months prior to the 7th day of August, 1930, they will find some reasons why the economic conditions in this country were as we found them on that day. Further, if they will study the exports of this country and observe that during the fifteen months before the 7th day of August, 1930, they began to dwindle, and if they will study the relation of imports to exports, they will realize the reasons that compelled this government to take the action it has done to repair the injuries to our economic structure which have resulted in the conditions to which I refer. To say, however, that these were wholly responsible for the conditions prevailing in this country would be unjust and unsound. In the past twelve months economic conditions throughout the world have grown gradually more acute. No normal legislation could have immediately and entirely offset them. It therefore becomes necessary for parliament to meet the situation, in so far as :t lies within its power so to do, by legislation specially designed for this abnormal situation. This government has had under the most careful consideration the means most likely to achieve that purpose, and has come to the conclusion that the best way to strike

at the root of the present trouble is to accelerate the natural progress of development by immediately commencing upon the construction of some such public works as will inure to the benefit of Canada. This program of national upbuilding is known to parliament and the country. The Conservative party was pledged to it in the campaign of last year, and after I was called upon to form a government I reaffirmed that pledge. When parliament met in the month of March last it was hoped that the amelioration of world conditions and a bountiful harvest in this country would, before the winter, result in a situation readily improveable by the measures of economic reform which have been passed. While that hope was possible of fulfilment, wisdom counselled the strictest conservation of our national revenues.
1 need hardly point out that the 120,000,000 that we voted in September last has given employment up to the end of July to upwards of 310,000 people, and it has resulted in contracts outstanding and work being done to the extent of some $70,000,000, scattered over every part of Canada, and every one of the undertakings assisted by that grant may be considered a work for the advantage of Canada as a whole, commencing with half a million for subways and going all down the line of public works, including road building. The amount expended for direct relief- I say direct relief-has not exceeded $2,000,000. It has not reached that sum. Under the cir-custances I think it will be realized that the national character of the relief afforded, which would be the only justification of our participating in relief operations at all, has been abundantly shown by the results which have been attained. But, as I have said, when we found this year that there was hope of an abundant harvest wTe realized that the conservation of our revenues was a duty of the first magnitude so far as this parliament was concerned, and we acted accordingly and awaited the harvest. But alas! for the second and even the third season the crops of the west have in large part been ruined by lack of moisture. During the last three weeks there was such an improvement as warranted the belief that there might be substantial quantities of green feed, for instance, available to take care of the stock and herds of those who live upon the prairies. But even that hope is now apparently destroyed, for the very scorching suns of the last few days have entirely changed that picture.
World conditions too, have since grown worse. The harvest as I have said, is in part a failure. In the opinion of the government therefore the circumstances justify an early

Farm and Unemployment Relief
expenditure of a sum of money which normally would have been spread over a period of years. Such moneys do not come from current revenues, and I believe a judicious outlay now will not be reflected adversely in the revenues of the country in the next few years. This, as I say, is a departure from settled procedure and practice based on our program, as we prepared it, from anticipated revenues. Normally it would not be justified, but under present conditions no true Canadian can cavil at it because it means increased employment, comforts and happiness to thousands of our citizens in the coming winter who would have had to go without the necessities of life. Nor need prudent citizens be unduly concerned over proposed expenditure; this country is solvent. If our people are assured of health, happiness and the means of livelihood, no capital disbursements, unless wantonly made, can impede our national fortunes built up by hard and intelligent working out of the vast riches which are our heritage.
I think everyone within sound of my voice to-day will agree with those propositions. Anyone, however, can be optimistic in good times. Optimism in bad times is bred of courage, faith and the capacity to endure. These are the dominant characteristics of Canadians. Not that I would urge the people of this country to nurture unfounded hopes; anxious times are yet ahead, and hard work and patience tad self denial are needed to bring good times out of them. But I hold that if we steadfastly maintain our belief in our destiny, which we do, and are prepared to meet the future with courage, which we are, then in this testing time we may fortify ourselves with the knowledge that following close upon the condition of to-day will come an era of true prosperity, fore-ordained, to those who have not swerved in their faith to themselves and to their country.
The pioneers of this country had to make for themselves their homes, and they had practically to provide from the soil, the sea, the rivers and the forests the wherewithal to enable them to live. We have lived in easier times. But we must fortify ourselves with the thought that the courage of the pioneers was never more required than now, and there never has been a time when faith in the ultimate destiny of our country was more required than it is to-day among the Canadian people.
The government realizes however that no matter how comprehensive this constructive program may be there will remain those who cannot directly benefit from it. That is,
there are those who may not benefit from constructive works carried on by the federal authorities with the provinces, and through the provinces with the corporations, towns and cities of the country. There are classes within the community who cannot work or for whom suitable work cannot be provided. These classes the government will assist either through the instrumentality of the provinces, and either public or private institutions, as may seem best, and in such ways as may seem most likely to assure the greatest measure of relief. No one will be asked to accept direct relief for whom suitable work can be procured.
During the last few days I have received telegrams from the province of Saskatchewan suggesting that it was not desirable that direct relief which might be regarded as charity should be accorded to those hardy settlers who have lost their all for the third, and in some instapces the fourth succeeding year, but rather that they would like to execute some document which would indicate that they regarded the help given as an obligation which they might some time be able to pay. I would say to my good friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan) that that indicates at least the attitude of most of those who at the present time are without crops and who have had the third succeeding crop failure.

speechtext:
Quite so. Nobody will be permitted to accept direct relief who is able to undertake work which is offered to him.	I need hardly say that even at this
early date in the history of this country there are not lacking evidences of an unwillingness to work on the part of those who believe that this country should give them money for nothing. The other day a parade came up this hill, and I had taken the trouble to make some investigation with regard to it. One at least of the participators in the parade the day before had been driving a Ford car, soliciting charity from various homes in other parts of this city. His conversations on those occasions are a matter of record. In every part of this country there are some evidences of that, already,-that is, evidences

Farm and Unemployment Relief
of a willingness to accept from the state charity, and charity from private sources as well, rather than to work. So the principle upon which we endeavour to proceed and will proceed is that where there is work there will be pay, and that if an individual is capable of work and will not work there will be no benefits. If there be those who think to increase the public burdens by unfairly casting themselves upon the state it will be our duty to make them as self sustaining as circumstances will permit. The people's money is not for those who are able but unwilling to care for themselves. I warn them of that now. The measures we shall take will be denied their fullest benefit without the generous cooperation of all classes in the land. Upon that cooperation we confidently rely. If any deny that cooperation, then they cannot properly look to us for support.
In that regard the measure provides for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada. It is not for a moment to be thought that an insignificant number of strongly vocal persons shall be able so to affect the populace of this country as to make it impossible for us, in cooperation together as Canadians, 'to work out our destiny. I say that class, happily, is few in number. But in this present situation they now see an opportunity propitious to the prosecution of their pernicious political doctrines. This is a land of freedom where men may think what they will and say what they will, so long as they do not attack the foundations upon which our civilization has been built. But as we have freedom, so have we justice, and it is not just nor right that now or at any other time we should permit such action by words or deeds as may tend to unsettle confidence in the institutions and customs under which we live. Most of our legislation is framed upon that assumption. For instance, the Naturalization Act provides for the cancellation of naturalization certificates where by act or speech the individual has indicated that his purpose is to create disaffection in the minds of those to whom his speech may be directed. If in times past we have had recourse to the provisions of that act, and will have in the future, it is because we realize that although they are few in number who thus attack our institutions and who in the name of free speech imperil the very existence of those institutions, it is not proposed that in a time of crisis and peril such as the present they should be permitted to make it more difficult for those who would cooperate to work for the common good. If the government is given 
reason to believe, as there may be some cause for its so believing, that there is a settled purpose in the minds of a considerable number of people-not large, numerically, but scattered over the various parts of Canada-to take action against the maintenance of law and order, or make attempts to impede the difficult task with which we are charged, then we will take such action as in the judgment of the executive of this country, the cabinet who are the board of directors for the time being administering the affairs of this country, as will free this country from those who have proved themselves unworthy of our Canadian citizenship.
I have said, sir, that the resolution does not contemplate the fixing of an amount that should be expended. It would be difficult indeed at this time to indicate with any degree of precision the exact sums that may be required to be expended for the public good. For that reason someone has said that the government asks for a blank cheque. It is not that. We ask between now and the expiration of t'he next fiscal year that the board of directors of this country, charged as it is with responsibility, and with a deep sense of its responsibility, shall discharge its duties from a financial standpoint as it best can and take the chances that are incident to so doing by submitting an account of its stewardship to this parliament before the 31st day of March next. That is the position we take with respect to the matter. It is nothing new. I was thinking yesterday, when someone was making an observation akin to criticism of the governor in council being permitted to have a large discretion as to the amount that may be expended for the purposes in question, that only a few short years ago my friends who now sit opposite, and who then constituted the government of this country, passed a statute, chapter 58 of the statutes of 1924, in Which they gave to the governor in council the power to guarantee the bridge bonds of the Montreal harbour commissioners. In the parliament of that day it was said that the cost would be $6,000,000. Did they put any limitation on the bill that gave that power to guarantee? They did not. In the province of Quebec it was said that the cost would be $10,000,000. Yet there are now outstanding on that bridge bonds for $19,000,000.

subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext: Would not a limitation have been desirable?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext:
I am only pointing out that no such limitation was imposed, and that those who criticize with respect to a matter which affects the welfare of the public cannot

Farm and Unemployment Relief
very well do so on any ground of consistency in view of the position that we know now follows with respect to that undertaking, where $19,000,000 of bonds are outstanding, issued without limitation, pursuant to the provisions of chaper 58 of the statutes of that year.
Would a limitation now be desirable? I have a telegram from one of the western premiers, who, having seen the resolution in. the papers, congratulates the government on imposing no limitation, for the simple and obvious reason that otherwise there would be a contest between the provinces to get their "share" as they call it, of what may be appropriated, and he regarded anything of that character as being inimical to the best interests of the administration of the money. I can only repeat that that view, so far as we have been able to ascertain, is the view held by the major number of those charged with responsibility in the provinces. I can say with great frankness to this house that I have no desire, and no other member of the government has any desire, to incur expenses or create obligations of the country out of keeping with the position which we occupy. But we believe that it is in the. interests of Canada-of the Canadian taxpayer, of the provinces, of the people concerned, that we Should not place a limitation upon the amount that may be expended, either with respect to direct relief or otherwise, because in the one instance you create the idea "Here is a fund upon which anyone may draw without work, and we have a right to live upon this fund that the taxpayers have so provided." And on the other hand you would have a contest among the provinces to get all that they believed to be their "share." We desire to administer the affairs of this country at this critical time having regard to the necessities existing in each part of this Dominion. There is one province, we will say, in which you could not if you chose expend more than $15,000 or $20,000 for any purpose that should come within the purview of this proposed statute. Then there is another province in which, as I have pointed out to this house, it is not improbable that there may be as many as 25,000 families that will have to be provided for.
Nor do we in undertaking our obligations desire to supplant the constitutional responsibility of the provinces. That constitutional responsibility must still be discharged. All we are endeavouring to do is to assist those charged with that responsibility to a due and adequate discharge of it. We are not substituting this Dominion for the provinces under the constitution; we are not substituting this
Dominion for the municipalities or towns under the constitution; but we are endeavouring, and we will continue to endeavour, to give such assistance to the constituted authorities in the several provinces as will enable them with such supervision as we think necessary in the public interest, to safeguard the public exchequer and ensure the three purposes that I have indicated, namely; work for those who are willing to u'ork-and pay there will be for none unless they who can work do work; and secondly, as I said a moment ago, relief for that class to whom work in the ordinary acceptance of the term may not be easily provided'-that is, people of the type who by reason of invalidity or other causes are not able to work; and there is that other class to which I referred, namely, those who have no opportunity at all in the circumstances under which they live to find employment of any kind.
I will say frankly to the house that in asking what euphemistically is spoken of as a "blank cheque" we are not unmindful that we are asking very considerable from this House of Commons. But how otherwise could we discharge the functions and responsibilities that devolve upon us? That is the question. If you fix it at an}' sum you may suggest, I repeat, you but invite the very thing that we desire to prevent, and by so doing instead of serving the public interest we are preventing the greatest service being rendered that the means available are intended to render.
In that regard I think it but fair to say to the house that we have already taken active steps in all the provinces. Commencing at the western coast, the provincial government of British Columbia has prepared a very full and definite program as to what it believes can be done with the assistance of the federal authorities to meet the unemployment situation during the winter. A large number of unattached single men have gone into the great city of Vancouver. That imposes upon the local authorities a burden of great magnitude. Almost every train has taken men into that city. If the provincial government in working out its plans with our financial cooperation and assistance, with such supervision as may be necessary to ensure that the money is not wasted, will make it possible for a large number of these unattached men who have collected in Vancouver to go out of that city and find employment elsewhere, we propose to enable them to do so. With respect to other cities in the central provinces, the same situation prevails and will be met in the same way.
The province of Alberta has prepared a comprehensive program of public under-

Farm and Unemployment Relief
takings. The province of Saskatchewan stands in a class by itself, for the reasons I have already indicated. The province of Manitoba has completed provision for a winter program which it believes will meet the situation. In the province of Ontario there are some signs already of what the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) indicated in the telegram he received from Kitchener, which showed a state of mind reflected in similar telegrams I have received from other Ontario cities, looking to this government to deal directly with them with respect to the problem of direct relief in those municipalities, towns and cities. We have endeavoured to make it clear that if we were to do so in the sense they have suggested we would be indeed breaking down their constitutional privileges and rights and substituting this Dominion for the constitutional authority provided for the very purpose they mention. We do not propose to do that.
In the province of Quebec the letter which was published the other day from the premier of that province made clear his position. In the maritime provinces they have prepared what they believe is an adequate program to meet the situation with which they must deal during the winter. In the province of Prince Edward Island, which has a population of less than 90,000, which is peculiarly an agricultural population, the difficulties are very few because they are not in want, as other parts of the country are, for reasons which are apparent to all.

speechtext:
Hon. members have before them a copy of the orders of the day on which appears the resolution which you, Mr. Speaker, have just read to the house. They will observe that if no reference is made to either the committee of supply or the committee of ways and means, this resolution constitutes the only order upon the order paper. It is not only the last government order to appear, but it is the only order which remains to be disposed of on the order paper to-day.
Perhaps I cannot better express in a word what' I have first to say in the way of criticism than to observe that, instead of being the last order in the last week of the session, this resolution should have been the first ordfer to appear after parliament assembled.

When we have regard to the circumstances of the past year, to the fact that a special session of parliament was thought necessary last September to deal with the question of unemployment, and that when parliament met in the month of March this year the unemployment situation was infinitely worse than it was when that special session was called, I do think it was the duty of the ministry to have made the question of unemployment relief the first, as indeed it is the most important question before this house and the country to-day. But far from bringing the matter forward at the beginning of the session, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has so managed affairs in the house as to have made impossible any discussion of the subject until now.
My right hon. friend has spoken of the cabinet as a board of directors, and he says that in this resolution he is asking the house to give to that, board of directors absolute powers in dealing with the problem of unemployment relief. May I say to him that it is not the cabinet, of which he is Prime Minister, that is the board of directors of the nation; it is this House of Commons. Hon. members sitting on both sides of the house are the board of directors who have been sent from the different constituencies in Canada to represent the people of the country, to discuss questions of importance with respect to the economic and other affairs of Canada, and to make laws to aid in the solution of those problems. The cabinet is a committee of the House of Commons; any power it has is derived from the members who sit in this house. It is an executive committee. But the committee of the nation constituting the board of directors is, I submit, this House of Commons. That leads me to direct again a very strong criticism against my right hon. friend. The criticism is this: that with regard to this all-important question he has ignored altogether the board of directors of the nation and has taken it into the hands of a small committee, which derives its authority from this board of directors, to deal with the question in an absolute way.
May I, to confirm what I have said regarding the extent to which my right hon. friend has prevented parliament from considering this question, mention a few records which appear in Hansard, of demands that have been made from time to time to deal with the question. I will not refer either to the debate on the address or to the budget debate. In each of these debates, which were of considerable length, hon. members on thi3 side spoke very freely with reference to this all-important question of the need for the

Farm and Unemployment Relief
relief of unemployment. But my right hon. friend and hon. members opposite were more or less silent; they made no contribution whatever to those debates. Indeed, during the greater part of the debate on the address my right hon. friend was not even present to hear what was being discussed. Here may I say that I think my right hon. friend has taken an entirely wrong course. Is it to be imagined that in regard to great problems such as unemployment relief, out of the number of members assembled here coming from all parts of this country-and I am speaking now with reference to those on the government side as well as on this-there would not be, in the course of a discussion on this question, some contribution which would be helpful to the ministry of the day? The purpose of parliament is to enable hon. members who live in different parts of the country to assemble in one place and there speak freely with respect to conditions in their particular constituencies, in that way to inform and enlighten the ministry with respect to existing needs and possible methods of dealing with them. But in respect to the greatest question of the day all that has been entirely set at naught, and now in the last days of the session, when, as all hon. members know, the proceedings are likely to be concluded within a day or two, we are for the first time afforded an opportunity to discuss this question.
On March 20 the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) asked the ministry if any special measures were contemplated to cope with the unemployment situation. The Prime Minister declined to answer. I am making reference now to matters of which full particulars will be found in Hansard.
On March 23 the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) asked what the government intended to do with regard to relieving the unemployed in his constituency. The Prime Minister said:
The question can stand.
On March 31 the hon. member for North Winnipeg moved the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely, the acute distress arising from unemployment. After a lengthy discussion Your Honour ruled the motion out of order.
On April 17 the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River brought up the question again, and failing to get a satisfactory answer from the government, he moved the adjournment of the house. This motion was defeated on division by eighty-two to fifty-six.
On April 24 the hon. member for Bow River (Mr, Garland) asked whether the government intended to call a Dominion unemployment conference. The Prime Minister said:
The hon. member will be advised when the event happens, if it does happen.
On May 25 the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) directed the attention of the acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) to the desperate condition existing in the city of Nanaimo, due to unemployment, and urged the government to deal with the situation immediately. The acting Minister of Labour said that the matter was purely a provincial one.
On May 26, on the motion to go into committee of supply, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni discussed the urgent necessity of holding a conference with the provinces to deal with unemployment. A lengthy debate followed during which the various speakers called upon the government to state its attitude towards the question. No member of the government took part in the debate.
On June 8 the hon. member for Comox-Alberni brought the question to the attention of the government once more, and called upon the ministry to declare its intention not only for the immediate future but also for the coming fall. The deputy speaker ruled him out of order, and on division the chair was sustained by sixty-four to forty-five.
On June 16, speaking on the budget, I urged the government to call a conference of all parties in interest to deal with the question of unemployment, but. neither in the course of that debate nor since was any reference made by any member of the ministry to the suggestion.
On June 29 the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked for a statement of government policy on unemployment. The Prime Minister replied:
At an appropriate time a statement will be made. The primary duty with respect to unemployment does not rest with the federal government.
Mr. Speaker ruled against the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in his attempt to continue the debate.
On June 30 the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) directed attention to the appalling conditions in Saskatchewan, and called upon the government to do something at once. The Prime Minister said:
The primary responsibility rests with the municipal authorities and the province.
On July 9, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) asked when



Farm and Unemployment Relief
the government would introduce legislation on unemployment. The Prime Minister said that legislation would be introduced when the business of the house had been practically disposed of. Immediately following his reply I said:	'
I assume my right hon. friend will he introducing some legislation in this connection, and I hope he will not wait until the last day or two of the session to place upon the order paper the resolution which would necessarily precede a bill to relieve unemployment. Hon. members ought to have a little time to consider any provisions before they are called upon to pronounce their view's.
The Prime Minister said that every opportunity would be afforded to discuss such a measure.
Those are only a few of the references that might be made. Hon. members will see that this resolution is introduced in 'the last days of the last week of the session, when there is no opportunity adequately to consider a measure so all-important.
May I say a word with respect to the resolution itself? In order to make clear the points that I wish to direct to the attention of the ministry, let me read the resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to unemploy'inent and farm relief; and for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada; and to authorize the governor in council to expend for the said purposes out of the consolidated revenue fund such sums as may from time to time be necessary.
I shall be pleased if my right hon. friend will allow' me to speak to him more particularly at this time.

speechtext:
My words will speak for themselves. If hon. members wish to laugh, that .is their privilege, but the public w'ill judge from what I am saying whether the proposals are in the interest of the government as well as of the country.
My first point is this: The resolution is really three resolutions embodied in one. I believe my right hon. friend would help materially in bringing about unanimity so far as the house is concerned^-and that is what I think we all desire in a matter of this kind- if he would divide his resolution into three
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
parts and deal as separate and independent measures with the three subjects to which it refers. The first resolution is with respect to the relief of unemployment:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to unemployment relief.
Unemployment relief is a subject by itself. It is the subject with respect to which a special session of parliament was called last September. I do not think w'e should confuse what relates to the relief of unemployment arising out of economic conditions with any other particular subject with w'hich the government wishes to deal.
The next subject in the resolution is farm relief. To make my point clear, may I say that until the crop failure in Saskatchewan and the distressing conditions existing in that province had become apparent, there was no thought in the mind of anyone that relief in the rural districts of the prairie provinces would be necessary. The situation in Saskatchewan has grown out of what I suppose would be described as an act of Godi It is in no sense due to any world condition or to any national policy, fiscal or otherwise. It is due simply to the happenings of nature as they have this year evidenced themselves. I submit that a measure to deal with Saskatchewan and the prairie situation generally to relieve a condition arising from crop failure should be a separate measure. After all, when we are dealing with these great economic questions it is important that the nation should know with respect to the different matters on which it spends its public moneys, precisely what its outlay is. The moneys .that are spent for relief in connection with Saskatchewan should be separately dealt with and separately administered, and similarly the moneys spent with respect to unemployment generally ought to be separately dealt with.
But the third is a still more important matter. The resolution reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada.
There is a third subject which is entirely separate and distinct from relief, either farm relief or unemployment relief generally. May I say to my right hon. friend that it is a great mistake to confuse these two matters. It is in every way most unfortunate that they' should be confused in any particular. We have laws on the statute books at the present time for the maintenance of law, order and good government throughout the country. If those laws are not adequate and my right hon. friend

Farm and, Unemployment Relief
wishes to have additional powers-to maintain law and order in Canada, let him ask for them in a separate measure. He is responsible for the administration, and if he says to this house that he has reason to believe that the powers that exist at the present time are not adequate to cope with any possible situation with respect to the maintenance of law and order in Canada, I will accept his word and support him in any reasonable measure he may bring down for that purpose. But I do say that he should not confuse any question of the maintenance of law and order with the question of unemployment relief or farm relief. Unemployment is an inevitable risk of industry. It is one of the unfortunate incidents of industry. It is bad enough for those who are unemployed to have to endure something for which they themselves are not at all responsible, but I do submit that it adds, if I may use an old-time expression, insult to injury to associate with the question of unemployment and relief for the unemployed any measures for the maintenance of law, order and good government in this country. Surely it is not fair to the thousands of men and women who find themselves without work through no fault of their own. but owing to conditions that are unavoidable so far as they are concerned, some of them owing to world conditions, some of them owing to fiscal policies, some of them owing to the distressed conditions of the prairies, to say that a measure submitted to parliament for their relief, should confer upon the governor in council additional power to deal with peace, order and good government in Canada. I am going to ask my right hon. friend to eliminate that particular clause from his resolution. I would ask him to do it in the interest of the very subject that he mentions, namely, peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada. I do not think it will make for peace, order and good government to include that particular clause in a resolution dealing with unemployment relief. Let that particular clause be eliminated, and then if for reasons that he may have in his own mind, my right hon. friend says, as I believe he sincerely thinks is the case, that there is need to give the governor in council additional power to deal with this question, let him bring in a measure for that purpose, and I think I can promise him the support of hon. members on this side. But I do submit to him very earnestly that he remove that clause altogether from his resolution and from the bill that may be based upon it. That is the criticism I have to make of the resolution in that regard.
May I next point out the difference between this resolution and the resolution upon which 22110-2721
the bill was based that was introduced during the special session of parliament in September last? At that time many of us thought that resolution went pretty far, that it gave the government considerable powers, gave them, not a blank cheque, but a very large cheque. We were inclined to be critical of the resolution on that ground, though we took no exception to the amount which my right hon. friend needed, and we allowed the resolution to pass. The resolution with regard to unemployment relief at the special session of parliament was as follows:
That it is expedient to provide that a sum not exceeding twenty million dollars be appropriated and paid out of the consolidated revenue fund for the relief of unemployment in constructing, extending or improving public works and undertakings, railways, highways, etc., that will assist in providing useful and suitable work for the unemployed, all as set forth in a bill founded on this resolution.
That resolution is direct to the purpose for which it was intended: That it is expedient to provide the sum of $20,000,000 to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund for the relief of unemployment. But this resolution is not specific in the same way with respect to the causes for which it is intended. This resolution is to give the governor in council increased powers, or as I say, absolute powers, to withdraw from this parliament altogether its control over the moneys to be expended and other matters, and to give that power to the governor in council. Here is the wording of the present resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council.
Then it goes on to enumerate the powers. That is a very different resolution, as I have said, from the one of a year ago. My right hon. friend and his colleagues would have been much better advised had they followed the resolution of a year ago-though it went very far-and adopted it as a precedent instead of going from bad to worse by now seeking to get absolute powers to themselves for these purposes. That would have removed our greatest objection to this measure. We are not going to object to the moneys that may be needed for unemployment and farm relief so long as parliament, the board of directors representing the people of this country, has its control and its say with respect to the expenditure. But we will object as strongly as we possibly can to increasing the powers of the governor in council in the matter of giving them unlimited authority with respect to public funds.
When I read the present resolution I thought to myself: "This has a familiar sound to it,
4286	COMMONS
Farm and Unemployment Relief
but not one that relates itself to times of peace. It reads to me like a war measures act." I went to the library of parliament to secure a copy of the war enactments, to see what legislation was passed, what authority was given to the government, and what action was taken by the government under that authority. I have before me an act to confer certain powers upon the governor in council and to amend the Immigration Act, assented to on the 22nd of August, 1914. This act may be cited as the War Measures Act, 1914. Section 3 of that act reads as follows:
The provisions of sections six, ten, eleven and thirteen of this act shall only be in force during war, invasion, or insurrection, real or apprehended.
Clearly indicating that the parliament of that day felt that the powers under the sections I have just mentioned would not be appropriate powers to ask from parliament in times of peace, that they should be in force only during war, invasion, insurrection, real or apprehended. Section 6 is one of the sections so mentioned. It reads as follows:
The governor in council shall have power to do and authorize such acts and things, and to make from time to time such orders and regulations. as he may by reason 9f the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion, or insurrection deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, it is hereby declared that the powers of the governor in council shall extend to all matters coming within the classes of subjects hereinafter enumerated, that is to say:-
The governor in council would have power to- deal with all the following matters if again empowered with the same powers given under the War Measures Act:
(a)	Censorship, and the control and suppression of publications, -writings, maps, plans, photographs, communications and means of communication:
(b)	Arrest, detention, exclusion and deportation;
(c)	Control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters of Canada and the movement of vessels;
(d)	Transportation by land, air or water, and the control of the transport of persons and things;
(e)	Trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture;
(f)	Appropriation, control, forfeiture and disposition of property and of the use thereof.
I need not read the other powers given, but I wish to direct the attention of the house to the fact that in this resolution my right hon. friend is asking for precisely the same powers by way of additional authority to the governor in council as those asked of this parliament in the War Measures Act.

Let me read part of the resolution as it stands with respect to the maintenance of peace, order and good government, and then read again the section from the War Measures Act, omitting the words, "by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection." The resolution is:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to unemployment and farm relief; and for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada;
That is the resolution before us. Section 6 of the War Measures Act is as follows:
The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may . . . . deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada.

No. My right hon. friend has said -that he has left out the word "defence"; that there is nothing concerning security and defence. I shall confine myself to the words which in intent are identical in the resolution and the act. In the act I find the w'ords:
The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations as he may .... deem necessary or advisable for .... peace, order and welfare of Canada.
That is practically the identical wording in 'both instances. On the one hand we have a War Measures Act, and on the other a peace time measure relating to the relief of unemployment and distress. In the War Measures Act it is expressly stated that the provisions of the section I have just read shall be enforced only during war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended. So I repeat to my right hon. friend that I do think he would be well advised to eliminate altogether that clause from the resolution dealing with unemployment relief. It would be most unfortunate-indeed one can scarcely say what might result from the inclusion of words through which the unemployed of the country may have reason to feel, for any cause whatever, that those particular words had been put in concerning their condition.
My right hon. friend has made clear in his speech that it is not with respect to the unemployed that he wants this particular power. He has said there is a noisy minority that may stir up a great deal of trouble in Canada and take advantage of the distressed .conditions to make additional trouble. He has said that he wants power to deal with

them. So long as there is a certain control with respect to taxation, which it is the obligation of this house above all others to guard, there will be, I believe, an attitude of generosity on the part of hon. members in the house to go a very great length in allowing the ministry wide latitude in such matters. However when the ministry goes a step farther and asks not only that they shall be free to spend moneys which are to be voted by parliament and are to come out of the taxes of the people, but that they are to be free to borrow to any extent to do whatever they like, all of which means more in the way of taxation, 1 think they are going a very great length and are creating a situation which it is impossible for the House of Commons to countenance, if it is at all to maintain its position as representing the people of Canada and controlling the expenditures of . the nation.
I can see where my right hon. friend may have difficulty in fixing an amount. He has given as his reason for wanting a blank cheque and not fixing a definite amount that a stipulated amount might lead to something in the way of competition or dole. May I say to him that if that is a true argument with respect to a limited amount, the force of the argument is vastly increased if the government is to be given a blank cheque. What is there to prevent the dole system becoming inevitable if the government has power to borrow and to spend as much as it pleases to relieve unemployment. By such a measure my right hon. friend is simply inviting the dole. There is no control of any kind the ministry can assert. The ministry can no longer assert, which is the strongest of all positions it can take, that parliament itself has not given it authority to go that far. It is relieving itself entirely of that restraint and saying to the country at large, "We have power to borrow all that we wish; we have unlimited power to use those borrowings for purposes of unemployment relief

in any way that we like." Nothing of that kind has ever existed in this country before.
I am not at all sure that even during the war for war purposes parliament gave the ministry any such unlimited powers. I do not believe parliament did. Certainly in time of peace this parliament cannot afford to go farther in matters of extending powers to the governor in council than parliament would have been prepared to go in time of war. I say I can realize where my hon. friend has difficulty in limiting his amount. That difficulty comes I think among other things from the large sum he fixed last year as that which he believed to be necessary to deal with the unemployment situation as it was then existing. We on this side did our best to have him realize that it was advisable to fix an amount that would serve up to the time that parliament reassembled, that the public would not distinguish between a sum of money which was put in the estimates last September and which could be spent over a prolonged period from a sum which would be just sufficient for the fiscal year and until parliament reassembled. But my right hon. friend wished to have large figures and he asked for S20,000,000.
To give the house a realization of what that sum of money meant in relation to relieving unemployment, may I recall the circumstances after the great war when the soldiers were returning and were being reestablished in civil life. At that time there were large numbers of unemployed, and that was the beginning of such relief. It was not under the Liberal administration, it was under the administration o-f the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, when the present Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson) held the same portfolio. At that time there was a great deal of unemployment and the minister laid down the policy that unemployment relief was a matter, first, for the municipalities, then for the provinces, and finally it became a dominion responsibility where the emergency was large enough to be a national one. That is the ground on which unemployment relief has been given ever since. We took the same position when we were in office with respect to unemployment relief. I made it quite clear that when these conditions existed we were prepared to deal with them as the former administration had dealt with them. But how much money was found necessary to meet the unemployment situation, grave as it was at that time, and grave as it was for some years after? Yet my right hon. friend with these figures before him asked parliament at the last special session to vote $20,000 000 for unemployment relief. Not all of that $20,000,000 has been spent, but the public have that figure in mind. Now my right hon. friend is in this position, that having at a special session started ivith an outlay of $20,000,000 for a certain period, he finds it difficult at the present time to know what particular amount to fix.
Now, may I say this to him? So far as the opposition is concerned, we will be prepared to allow him to make any estimate he likes, so long as it is an estimate based on good judgment, and we will not question that estimate, we will allow him to have the amount he asks for. But we do assert, if it is only for the sake of maintaining what is the most fundamental of all obligations of the Commons, namely, its control over expenditure, that he should not ask us to give him a blank cheque to borrow as much as he pleases to deal with this particular matter. That is our position in a word, and I would again very strongly urge my right hon. friend to modify the bill that he may introduce by fixing a definite amount.
Here may I say it is always possible to call parliament together. It was deemed all-important last September to have a special session when unemployment conditions were far from being as serious as they are at the present time. If a special session was necessary last September, and my right hon. friend cannot make an estimate as to what he is going to require to meet the situation ahead, if the situation is going to be so serious that larger amounts than the sum he may ask this parliament to vote will be necessary, then it seems to me it is not only his right, it is his duty to bring parliament in session and allow

parliament to deal with the greatest question that is before the country at the time. That is what parliament is for-to deal with questions that are all-important to the nation. My right lion, friend has now a breathing space, he has a clear road ahead of him, and if he asks for a sum of money, which doubtless will be sufficient to meet his purposes up to the end of the year, he can call a regular session of parliament early in January. And I think every hon. member on both sides of the house will thank him if he brings parliament into session in January rather than in March, or even in February. My right- hon. friend has said he will convene parliament in the middle of February. May I say to him that it would better suit the convenience of everybody if he would bring parliament into session early in January. Let him name the sum that he thinks necessary to meet the situation up to January, and we will give him what he asks. Then early in January if he needs further money let him ask for it, and I do not think he will encounter much in the way of opposition to what he considers is necessary to enable him to finish out his fiscal year. But I do say he is going altogether too far when he asks that he shall be free even of the sittings of parliament to deal with what is now, and, what he told us in his speech to-day, will be the most serious situation that Canada has been confronted with perhaps at any time in her history.
One other objection I have to this resolution. It offers no advance over the step which was taken at the special session of parliament. At the time of the special session we very strongly advocated that the whole question of unemployment relief should be put into the hands of an unemployment relief commission, which would have power to study carefully the wdiole situation, which *would be in touch with the provinces and the municipalities and which would be a body gathering information and knowledge as well as dealing with the situation which was before it. Had such a commission been appointed last September, and had it been given administration of the $20,000,000 which was placed at my right hon. friend's disposal, that commission would be in existence to-day and would know more or less exactly the position with respect, to every province and every municipality and would be able to advise the ministry and parliament what was necessary to meet the continuing situation. But all the good that might have been obtained from a permanent body created for that special purpose has been lost; although the money has been spent, there is nothing in the way
of further information upon which parliament can act. Speaking on the budget, I suggested that it was advisable immediately to call a conference of those parties that are likely to be best informed on the whole question of employment and unemployment, to bring together representatives of the provinces and of the leading municipalities, representatives of employers and of trade unions, representatives of agricultural associations and of boards of trade, representatives of women's organizations and of any other bodies that have to do with the forming of public opinion. I suggested that when that conference met they should choose a body that would be non-political in its character, and would constitute a commission for the purpose of dealing with unemployment relief. I suggested that the government might well place in the hands of a body of that kind the disposition of such funds as parliament might vote. On that body could be placed the expert men and women of this country, regardless of their politics, who understand social, industrial and economic conditions. They would be a body infinitely better qualified to deal with this question than the cabinet possibly could be, with its many other obligations and its particular duties what they are.
I still suggest that something of that kind should be done. I am not suggesting that any organization should be formed that would invade the jurisdiction of the provinces and the municipalities. What I would suggest is that a body of that kind should see to it that every province has its own organization along lines laid down by the federal commission as being the most advisable and desirable, and that each province should see that each municipality had its particular organization also to deal with the situation as it might affect that locality. In this way there would be something in the nature of uniformity and equal treatment throughout all parts of the Dominion. It is useless to say that a body of that kind could not be readily created. I remember very well when we were celebrating the diamond jubilee of confederation; there was a national committee which had to do with the arranging of the celebration throughout Canada. That committee arranged for each province to have its provincial committee, and each province arranged that each municipality should have its committee, and the result was that with respect to that particular celebration there was not one part of the Dominion which was not linked up with the great parent organization, and with respect to which the national organization had not full particulars.

A body of that kind dealing with unemployment relief would be of great national service. May I point out this further feature: We have been discussing at this session the question of unemployment insurance. I cannot conceive of a more useful fund of information to enable this parliament to deal with that question at a future session than that which could be gathered by a body of the kind. What are we to get in the way of information from all the millions that will be spent on unemployment relief under the method suggested by the Prime Minister? We will have nothing to show for it; the money will have been spent; certain employment will have been given, but the wide knowledge which might be obtained as to the causes of unemployment, the circumstances surrounding it and the like will have been lost entirely.
I do not wish to go again into the many points I raised at the special session with regard to these grants to the provinces from the federal treasury without adequate control over expenditure on the part of the federal parliament. In a word I will just say that what was said at the special session in that particular stands also by way of criticism of the resolution now before us in the form in which it has been brought down.
In conclusion may I say to my right hon. friend that in speaking on the budget I expressed, speaking not only on behalf of myself but as well for the entire opposition, a sincere desire to cooperate with the Prime Minister to the best of our ability in working out any plans which would help meet this serious situation in Canada as it exists at the present time. But my hon. friend is taking away from us any opportunity of cooperating with him at all when he asks us on almost the last day of the session, without any possibility of discussing plans at all, to give him a blank cheque to borrow what he wishes and then dismisses parliament for an indefinite period Our powers of cooperation as members of this house are definitely gone. By his resolution he virtually tells us that he does not thank us for our offer of cooperation and does not expect to receive anything in the way of helpful suggestion not only from the opposition but from members on his own side of the house. I think that is most unfortunate with respect to a situation as grave as the present one, and I can only regret that my night hon. friend makes it necessary for me to make that observation with regard to his method of dealing with the matter.
If, as my right hon. friend did, I might summarize in a word what I regard as the im-

portant points with respect to this resolution, I would say first of all that he should not seek to obtain all the powers he desires under this one resolution but should divide the resolution into three parts. I would suggest that he ask this house to vote a sum of money for unemployment relief; that he- ask the house to vote a sum for farm relief and that he ask us to enact whatever he may think necessary to give him additional powers for the maintenance of peace, law and order. That is the first point. Then having divided his resolution into three separate measures let him fix the amount with respect to each measure which he deems necessary to meet the situation from now until he may call parliament again. If he does this, speaking for the opposition I may say that we will let him take the responsibility in full for what he may feel to be necessary in regard to the amount for which he asks, and we will give him that full amount. But we cannot completely surrender the rights of this House of Commons and of parliament with respect to its control over expenditures for any purpose that may be named, and we cannot accord him our approval of the resolution in the form in which it has been brought down.

Mr. Speaker, from the standpoint of labour this is the most important measure of the session, and I am sure a large number of working people across the country will welcome the news that some definite provision is to be made for unemployment I quite agree with the Prime Minister that the object ought to be to provide work rathej than merely to give charity. Further than that, it seems to me an advance has been made over previous arrangements in the enunciation by the Prime Minister of the principle that the necessities of the several communities should be the governing factor in the administration of relief measures.
I think the Prime Minister made a mistake, however, when in his exhortation that we should have courage he went back to the pioneer days. It seems to me the comparison is very slight between the conditions in which men find themselves to-day and the conditions in which our grandfathers or great-grandfathers found themselves. The Prime Minister suggests that we live in easier times than they did. I am not at all sure that this is so. I have heard stories of pioneers, that they had to dig up the potatoes which they had planted and so on; I know they had to make for themselves shelters in the woods, but I point out to the Prime Minister that in the old days men had opportunities of go-

Farm and Unemployment Relief
ing into the newer parts of the country. They had an opportunity of taking up land for themselves; they had an opportunity of going from one place in which there was no work to another place where they might obtain work. They had an opportunity of going into the woods for certain seasons of the year. I would say that the conditions of the thousands of our people who are now riding the freight cars from industrial town to industrial town, finding no more work in the place to which they come than in the place which they left, are a great deal harder than the conditions any of our people had to meet in the pioneer days.
The Prime Minister suggested that certain men seemed to be willing to accept charity rather than work, and he instanced the fact that one among those who came here in the unemployed parade had been seen begging, and had been driving around in a Ford car. I am quite well aware that there are men who take advantage of conditions in almost every walk of life. But speaking by and large, the vast majority of the unemployed to-day are men who are willing to work, who have worked in the past, and who would be working now if anything like suitable employment were provided. We must recognize clearly, along with this, that if men are allowed to drift about from month to month for any long period they readily become unemployable and before long they will settle down into an undesirable class. But it is altogether unfortunate that the Prime Minister should suggest that any large number of these people are out of work because they are lazy or shiftless.

The Prime Minister has all along taken the ground that we ought to beware of the dole. But I would point out that this haphazard way of giving relief, of providing relief or jobs here, there and yonder just as necessity may arise, constitutes the very worst and most demoralizing form of the dole that could be invented. I believe the leader of the opposition has distinguished three measures that are herein included. In my study of the motion I discovered five distinct measures.
