speechtext:
Fifty cents a day
would be merely spending money. There is plenty of productive work to be done in this country and these men who find themselves out of work to-day have a right to be found work at a remunerative rate. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) said that he was in favour of giving pay only to those who would work. I suppose, in a general way, we are all agreed as to that. But I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he is willing to give decent wages to those who are willing to give good work? That is a matter-and an important one-upon which lie made no pronouncement. It is one in which the labour people across this country are very much interested. In passing may I say that it is rather curious that we have to go to the minister of a province to find out what the federal government intends to do, but that is the only place at the present lime to which we can go for information. The federal government has not announced its policy, so I presume some arrangements have been made with at least some of the provincial governments. Mr. Finlayson suggests there will be no relief given if the men refuse to stay in camp. That seems to be rather a serious situation; at least it might work out in a disastrous way. A little earlier in the session we heard a great deal about forced labour in Russia. I was rather interested in noting, according to a despatch in the Montreal Gazette of July 21, 1931, that a British group had investigated the charges made against the Russian lumber trade. The despatch reads:

Farm and Unemployment Relief
Members of the British trade delegation which spent three weeks inspecting the lumber centres of northern Russia returned to Moscow to-day with the statement that they had found no evidence to support charges that forced labour is used in the Russian lumber industries.
The despatch goes on to elaborate this statement. While we have been criticizing forced labour in Russia, which appears from investigation not to exist, we are in very great danger of establishing something like forced labour in northern Ontario and other parts of Canada. In other words, we will say to these unemployed men: You go into camp and do your work under whatever conditions we prescribe for practically no wages, and if you do not do that, you starve. That is a serious situation and those are serious conditions to impose upon any free people. In fact such a situation would differ very little from slavery.
Moreover it is actually being suggested in the newspapers that these camps should be placed under military control. I hope the government has nothing of that kind in contemplation, because I feel sure it would raise a storm of protest, not merely from all sections of labour but also from all thoughtful citizens. AVe ought not to set up detention camps in Canada in times of peace. It is a dangerous proceeding and it is not fair to those men who are unfortunate enough to be out of work.
I should like to say a word with regard to the transients. No one has these days very much good to say of them. They have been forced to adopt more or less the life of hoboes, but in past years they have done much of the hard work of building up this country, in the lumber camps, the construction camps, the harvest fields, the mining camps and so on. Everywhere in the early stages of the development of this country we have depended upon the now despised transient workers, and they ought, I think, to receive at least a decent living. I should like to emphasize the point of view that I have been trying to bring before the house, that a decent living to this class of men has a prior claim to the interest charges of the banks, or to the dividends of the bondholders in any of our corporations or even to the interest on government bonds. I do not think this can be too strongly impressed upon the house.
Especially ought this to be emphasized with regard to foreign labour. Undoubtedly we have admitted altogether too many aliens into this country, and I think we in our corner of the house have done our best during the
past ten years to protest against the immigration policy of the late government, a policy that I may say was endorsed pretty generally in the house and in the country at large. But now that we have these people here, we Should treat them decently. We have spent millions of dollars in trying to induce them to leave their homes in mid-Europe or Norway or Sweden and to come to Canada to throw in their lot with us. Some of them unfortunately have not been able yet to become naturalized, and when a time of crisis comes, because of their lack of knowledge of the English language and because of their lack of connections here, they are the first to be laid off and to suffer the most heavily. Nevertheless, they have taken their full share in doing the heavy work of this country, and I rvould urge that nothing be done at this time of crisis that would lead to injustice in our attitude towards those whom we have asked to join with us in building up a new country.
Think of the conditions under which many of these transients are forced to live. Some weeks ago I called attention to the bad conditions that existed in the east end of this city. I find that similar conditions exist in almost every large centre from coast to coast. In the Toronto Star of June 28, I find an article on the "Jungles of Toronto." I will read a paragraph or so:
Some five hundred residents of the Don valley, Toronto's unique residential quarter, were just getting up when the Star arrived to-day. Crawling out from huts and shacks which look for all the world like beaver colonies, men of every nationality, nearly all of them unemployed, started lighting breakfast fires, washing at the stream, or cleaning their teeth.
Homeless, these men have built for themselves "homes" from the flotsam and jetsam which clutters the valley in the vicinity of the Don valley brickyards. Dried burdock plants, sticks of wood, heavy wrapping paper, and branches of trees have been interwoven and thatched to make several colonies of the little shacks. Some of the men, who were termed "transients" by a well-spoken shack owner, were sleeping in the open, on sheets of rusty tin to prevent ground moisture from seeping through.
Sleeping in the brick kiln where the officials of the works have strung up electric lights for the use of the sojourners, are the men about twenty of them who have been in the valley all winter. They are very jealous of their prerogative of sleeping in the comparatively swanky and dry kilns. Further to the east, and strung out along the railroad tracks have grown up within quarter of a mile of Rosedale, the miniature village, a unique product of the current depression.
Except for the more or less permanent residents in the brick kiln, everything in the village is in a continual state of flux. "Gangs of fifty or sixty leave here every night on the freight trains, and about the same number drift in by the same means," one of them told the Star.

Farm and Unemployment Reliej
Conditions of that kind, which I say are typical of those in nearly all our cities today, are a disgrace to any civilization. Those old lines of Lowell's have frequently been running through my mind lately.
Think ye that building shall endure
Which shelters the rich and crushes the poor!
It seems to me that a time of depression of this kind brings upon us the absolute necessity of giving fair play to those who are perhaps the least influential members of our community.
Let me give a warning to the government. I believe if camps are established under anything like military control, they may become schools of bolshevism. It may be that the government may be able to increase its mounted police force and keep individual camps in order. It may be that they will call in the military, but again let me warn that the army may easily become a Haman's gallows, the means by which capitalism itself will be done to death. The authorities of the present order are undoubtedly in a dilemma. They may be damned if they don't, but certainly they will be damned if they do, and I hate to think of the suffering that may be involved.

speechtext: Who made the statements?

subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext:
They have been
common in all our papers. This is almost our last opportunity for protest. AVithin a few days parliament will prorogue, and then the members of this house will have no opportunity of making their protests in the house, and I do want to urge upon the government that they will not permit anyone to influence them to establish camps of that character.
There is a very great deal of constructive work that might be undertaken in this country, I think, of our highways, of reforestation, of tree planting on the prairies, which in part would help prevent the drifting of our soil, of clearing the land in many scrubby districts, of drainage, of preparing semi-ready farms and better homes for the settlers on the prairie, of level crossings, of improving our parks and clearing out our slums, and par-

ticularly I would say the slums in the great city'- of Montreal, and of providing decent homes and healthful surroundings for the people. Only the other day a gentleman who had just returned from Vienna was telling me of the wonderful housing schemes being carried on in that fine old city. It seems to me that our government might undertake something of this character.
Of course, the old question comes up, and I think the Prime Minister will be the first to raise it: how are you to finance such schemes? I would say that if the country is as strong as he would have us believe, we have the whole credit of the country upon which to draw. The Prime Minister would finance the schemes by drawing on the consolidated revenue fund, that is, by borrowing. I would point out to him that a few years ago there was a precedent set for another type of financing. In 1914 and 1915 the government issued currency to the amount of S26.000.0CIO, 510,000,000, if I recall aright, for the Canadian National railway, $6 000.000 for the Grand Trunk, and 810,000,000 for the treasury. I would suggest that a policy of that kind would mean that we would have the money without interest, and further than that, as my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) has pointed out, such a procedure would at the same time lessen our load of debt. That is no cheap money scheme, but at this time when we have some of the leaders in finance pointing out the necessity of policies of this character I think it would be wise that the government should carefully consider action along this line rather than continuing to borrow and thus burdening the country in the years to come with a load of debt.
The Prime Minister in this motion and also in his speech indicated that he desired greater power than is now possessed by the government to deal with those who would in any way imperil law and order. The Prime Minister said that he wanted such powers with a view to such action "as in our judgment" -I presume he meant in the judgment of the government-"will free this country of those who have not proved themselves worthy of Canadian citizenship." Again let me say that this seems rather in harmony with some of the statements that we have had recently in our newspapers. I noticed just recently an Ottawa despatch that appeared in the western newspapers, as follows:
Ottawa, July 7.-The federal government is planning a round-up of communists and revolutionists in all sections of Canada, but more particularly in the west. It is definitely established here to-day that there are a number of "Reds" in the Winnipeg district who have beer

Farm and Unemployment Relief
marked down for arrest and deportation, and action certainly will be taken before the summer is over.
As I have tried to say in this house before, I wish that I were not placed in the position where it would always seem as if I were defending all the actions of our local communists. I am not doing that. I think, however, there is a bigger question here, and that is the question of freedom. We are in danger of becoming hysterical. For example, in the Montreal Gazette of July 23, 1931, I find an interview given by Lieutenant-Colonel R. H. Webb, the mayor of my own city, from which I quote a few paragraphs:
Bolshevism's insidious "Group G" is getting a grip on Canada's recent immigrants, especially around Winnipeg, and the Dominion, hampered with a legal system that is not made to cope with such a situation ought to enforce a. national emergency measure, something like Great Britain's "Dora," or Defence of the Realm Act of war-time fame, Lieutenant-Colonel Webb said in response to a query on that subject.
Ordinary forensic methods were out of the question in dealing with bolshevik agents, he said. The Dominion ought to maintain a secret service expressly for combating the bolshevik menace, and ringleaders, instead of being hauled up in the ordinary law- courts and allowed to hire high-priced counsel, ought to be just spirited out of the country and back to where they came from.
Canada ought to take a leaf out of the American book of sedition, and place the matter in th e hands of the Immigration department, which is responsible for bringing foreigners into the country and making them into citizens, and of the federal police, who are here the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
It does seem to me an extraordinary thing, Mr. Speaker, that in times of peace we should have any citizen, to say nothing of the mayor of one of our large cities, telling us that ordinary forensic methods are out of the question in dealing with a certain section of our community and that we should adopt secret police methods and spirit these people out of the country without trial. I would say that anybody who makes such a statement is not only doing his best to foster bolshevism, but I think is copying directly what we denounce as bolshevist methods. If there is to be any deportation I would say that the mayor of Winnipeg might be the first to be deported for trying to introduce bolshevist methods into Canada. But I am glad to say that the position of our "travelling mayor" is not the attitude of a good many people in Winnipeg. For example, I had a letter the other day from the city clerk, enclosing a copy of a resolution passed in connection with the Alien Identification Card Bill, which I believe has been before the Senate. The resolution reads:
We, the members of the municipal council of the city of Winnipeg, are of the opinion that the "Alien Identification Card" bill now before the Senate of Canada will not accomplish the object sought by its sponsors, and tends to stigmatize newcomers to Canada. It is considered an undeserved insult by immigrants who came to this country with the best intentions of becoming, and are honestly trying to be, worthy Canadian citizens. We therefore urge the hon. members of the Senate and House of Commons not to press such legislation, but to maintain unsullied our Canadian ideals of civil equality and social justice.
May I repeat that last phrase, and I would urge upon the Prime Minister, that we should maintain unsullied our Canadian ideals of civil equality and social justice.
While I have had hundreds of communications from labour organizations across the country protesting against some of these proposed methods, I should like to read a paragraph from an editorial in the Manitoba Free Press of July 24, which I think represents fairly well the judgment of a large number of the citizens of my own community:
The communists may be imposing on the good nature of the community, and taking advantage of rights which their own creed, in its own country, would refuse to tolerate for a moment, but such action as the council takes with the communists must leave uninfringed the right of free speech exercised in Winnipeg.
Free speech cannot be allowed to come under police supervision or discretion, which is what would happen were police permits required before meetings could legally be held.
I feel proud to be a citizen of Winnipeg when one of our leading papers takes that attitude. Sometimes it seems to me that in adopting these rather haphazard measures the Prime Minister is facing a great conflagration with a little squirt gun. He is trying to put out the conflagration, and when anyone expostulates that he definitely promised to put out the fire he exclaims, in great indignation, "No, I promised to meet it. Time will tell how successful I will be," whereupon he works harder than ever with his squirt gun and the fire rages more furiously than ever.
Almost in despair he at this time seeks autocratic powers. Sometimes I have wondered how to characterize the position and methods of the Prime Minister. On occasions he seems to be the conductor of a great orchestra composed of the members of his own party. As conductor, however, he does not permit each member of the orchestra to play very long or very loud on his own instrument but he conducts as would the leader of a jazz orchestra showing his versatility by playing in turn on each instrument as it is passed up to him.

It seems to me that in this resolution not only have we auto-

cratic action, so far as the party is concerned, but the Prime Minister is taking the powers entirely out of the hands of parliament and placing them in his own and in those of his immediate colleagues. I think the situation is too dangerous for that. Further, may I venture to suggest that the world wide depression demands a great deal more in the way of constructive, far reaching planning.
I feel sure that the Prime Minister is sincere in the belief that his policies will solve our problems. I will say that he is almost fanatically sincere in that regard. Those of us however who have not his particular brand of fanaticism may be pardoned if we question his methods, when he asks us to hand all power over to him.
In closing may I say that while we have been talking to-day about unskilled workers, nothing whatever has been said about the skilled workers of whom there are very large numbers out of work, and for whom provision would not be made by the measures which have been indicated. Further, there are a very considerable number of women workers about whom very little has been said. The same is true of clerical workers who are perhaps in a more serious plight than manual workers. Last, I would point out the thousands of young people in this great land of opportunity who have not been given a chance as they left school to procure work. I cannot see that haphazard emergency methods, such as that now before us, are going to solve the problems of the classes which I have merely enumerated. Even now, before this house prorogues, might it not be possible for the government to reconsider the situation, take the house into its confidence and work out some sort of general plan, appoint a central committee which would not merely supervise the giving of relief-which in fact might not supervise the giving of relief it all-but which might study the underlying ;auses of unemployment and have the general direction and planning of what might be done to meet the situation.

subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext:
I do not purpose to delay the house at any great length, but I feel I should say a few words. With much that 'the speaker who has just taken his seat has said, I agree. With some of the criticisms by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), I agree. The unfortunate fact is that it does not matter very much what the leader of the opposition, the leader of the Labour group or myself may say in the present instance. I am convinced that for the purpose of meeting a crisis the government is determined to carry through its dictatorial and autocratic policy of usurping

the powers of the state. That the need for drastic action is there, I do not deny. There is no doubt under heaven that one of the most serious situations has arisen in Canada, and it is now proposed to meet it planlessly. The proposal before us in of a broad and general character. The amount of money involved we know nothing about; we do not know what will be spent., and I doubt very much if the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) himself has any comprehensive idea or estimate of the amount actually required. I doubt if he knows what works he will undertake. I suggested to him to-day one public work which might be proceeded with, but he replied that the engineers were not yet in agreement concerning that particular work. I do not think it would be a difficult matter, now that the surveys have been completed concerning the Peace River outlet, to have an agreement. I think action by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways and Canals would result in that very useful piece of work being proceeded with
Because of the refusal of the leader of the opposition himself, as well as the present Prime Minister, to accept recommendations made a year ago and in previous occasions by hon. members in this corner of the house, we find ourselves in the present unfortunate position. A year ago last May I closed my remarks on the unemployment debate by saying to the then Prime Minister that he would not have taken the first step towards the solution of this problem until he authorized a comprehensive survey of economic and social conditions in Canada, with a view to planning for the solution of those problems. Nothing was done; no such body was appointed nor has it been appointed by the present administration. There has been no survey. In a previous debate this session one of the ministers opposite suggested that such a survey could be undertaken by the census takers-an absurd proposition.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, if this government or the preceding one had been gifted with that vision, which ought to be a prerogative of statesmen-and Pr;me Ministers in particular-they would have seen this situation. All they had to do was to listen to and cany into effect -the suggestions of hon. members in this corner of the house, or to listen to the suggestions of such outstanding men with wisdom and brains as Sir George Paish, Lord d'Afoernon and others who forecast the present situation in regard to unemployment. The situation in Europe alone would have justified anybody assuming that such a condition would come about.

Farm and Unemployment Relief
What do we find? At the very outset of this session hon. members opposite, including the Prime Minister, attempted to minimize the seriousness of the situation, attempted to gloss over it. Then, on July 1, the Prime Minister made a pronouncement to the country more devastating in its gloomy forecast than anything that the people of Canada or hon. members in this house had heard of. He comes into the house to-day and by implication at least, if not by actual words, states that the situation has now become so desperate that nothing short of war measures could be calculated properly to deal with it. I doubt if there is any country in the world-* there is not one that I know of-which so far has found it necessary to undertake such drastic and far-reaching measures to meet the economic situation. In other words it would appear that the Prime Minister is now so exercised-and I congratulate him upon being troubled, even though he be late-that he is prepared even to usurp the powers of parliament itself and resort to what might virtually be termed a dictatorship for the purpose of meeting the situation. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I think he would be wise to meet the suggestion of the leader of the opposition to state a definite amount sufficiently large to cover every need anticipated, and then proceed with a general plan of constructive public works to give employment to those requiring it. To-day the situation is quite a bit worse than it was a year ago or even two years ago. In those days the contention that the constitutional position in dealing with unemployment was that the municipalities came first, the provinces second, and then the federal government; that contention was perhaps unassailable at that time. But now, as the Prime Minister himself would describe it, and in fact does describe it, we have a national calamity, a national crisis, so great in its magnitude that he is now prepared to ask parliament for these sweeping powers. The fact of the matter is the whole situation is now reversed, and instead of the municipalities bearing the first responsibility the federal government must do so. The Prime Minister himself accepted that position when, speaking on behalf of his party during the last election campaign, he said:
I will end unemployment, I will take such measures as will provide for the giving of work to every man and woman in this country prepared to work.
Now we find a measure introduced which, in part, is a proposal to provide public work -at what wages we do not know yet-and, in part, makes provision for the dole. That
is what it amounts to. I wish I could have some comprehensive idea of just exactly what is in the Prime Minister's mind. I do wish hon. gentlemen opposite had not made those statements they did make early in the session, when even the Minister of Labour himself, speaking in Hamilton on April 28 last, expressed these views:
In Canada the unemployment problem is diminishing. We have experienced the most distressing winter in many years, but we emerge into the sunlight of hope at the beginning of another season, and it is within the realm of reason to say that before the snow falls again our wories will have largely-disappeared.
The situation now is so bad that we need a war measures act to cope with. I congratulate the government, however, on proposing to meet the problem by providing work. I am afraid difficulties face the administration in this regard. If the government does succeed in meeting this problem with useful and remunerative work it will bo the first government that I know of that has ever been able to do so. All governments are agreed that the policy of providing work is the best, and so are all individuals who have studied the question. And after all, all the men ask is work or maintenance. But all governments on coming into power have one eye on the treasury and the other on the unemployment problem, and the result is that one is controlled by the exigencies of the other. In Great Britain the grave situation has not been met by comprehensive public works, but a great deal of direct relief has been provided; much the same situation prevails in Germany; much the same situation exists in the United States, where charitable organizations are the present resource of the unemployed, the starving, and the miserable.
I think the time has come, Mr. Speaker, when governments should reconsider their whole method of borrowing for purposes such as these, and I support most strongly the latter suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), when he submitted to the Prime Minister a plan for providing the necessary moneys for all public work that might be required to take up the slack of unemployment by simply issuing dominion notes on the basis-if he wants to go through that formality-of dominion bonds deposited with the treasury board. We do it for our chartered banks now; why not do it for the state? It is a sound, a reasonable proposal. We could do that without charging the state a single dollar of interest. The additional currency thus created could be repaid subsequently out
Farm and Unemployment Relief

of taxation. It appeals to me as a far superior method to borrowing money on longterm bonds and paying high rates of interest.
Before I sit down I want to call the attention of the Prime Minister to the demoralization due to the semi-starvation pay that is being given at the present time and during the last winter has been given to those who secure either direct relief or the inadequate work offered. In the city of Calgary, ior example, until quite recently unemployed single men were receiving meal tickets for one meal a day and a bed in return for one day's work. I do not need to invite hon. members opposite who will spend a dollar and a half on a single meal in the Chateau Laurier to imagine just what the life of these people must be. One meal is all they get a day, in return for which they have worked eight hours. Recently the regulations were altered, and now the men are asked to give two day's work each week for the same return-two day's work for one meal a day and a bed. And even at that, Mr. Speaker, the single unemployed men in the city of Calgary are in a superior position to the single unemployed men in most of the cities of this country, for with few exceptions there is no provision for unemployment relief for single men.
The next thing to which I want to draw the attention of the Prime Minister is the situation in Drumheller, in my own constituency. There the married people, unemployed since last spring, very slightly employed in the winter of 1929-30, and with practically no employment, or very little, in the winter of 1930-31, have been receiving $125 a week per adult, and 25 cents per week for each child, irrespective of age or size. Can you maintain the moral fibre of the citizens of t'he country on the basis of pay of that kind? I ask the Prime Minister, can he expect that optimism and faith and pioneering courage which he seeks in our people on pay of $1.25 a week for each adult and 25 cents a week for each child? It is nothing but slow starvation. That is the situation that has existed in connection with hundreds of people in my own constituency in the mining valley of the Red Deer. Recently as the result of constant agitation, as the result of parades and demonstrations, the single unemployed men in that vicinity secured a measure of relief-one dollar and a half a week for a full-grown man. All they ask, Mr. Speaker, is work. Here is a message sent to the premier of my province, by these very men who held a mass meeting of some thousand odd, over four hundred of whom paraded to the police station at Drumheller seeking relief:

Unless relief is immediately granted, workers must help themselves. They will not die at the time when warehouses are full of all kinds of food and other necessities of the workers. We have produced the wealth and we have the right to live.
Dangerous words, Mr. Speaker, for men in dangerous circumstances. We have the mayor of Edmonton emphasizing this in an emphatic prediction that we shall see, "Worse times than we yet have seen." His statement that the situation was getting beyond the power of the civic authorities to deal with deserves consideration at the hands of this house. According to the newspapers, after meeting Premier Brownlee and discussing the situation in Lethbridge, he said:
The situation in Lethbridge was acute and the costs to the city so high that it was the intention to cut off the relief April 26. At least 700 families in the city were in a state of destitution.
The- miners in the Drumheller valley-the Prime Minister is not .particularly interested, but I do not suppose it makes any difference- wired the premier of Alberta as follows:
We want work or full maintenance-
In order to make absolutely clear what they meant by "full maintenance" they added: -the latter meaning three meals a day and a place to sleep.
Surely every Canadian man and woman and child is entitled to three meals a day and a place to sleep.
We want no discrimination between single and married men and no eviction for nonpayment of rent while unemployed.
They complained that their light and water had been cut off and that they needed clothing. They preferred work to relief. It is the cry of every man who has anything real in him,-work, not relief.
There is just one other matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the Prime Minister. I have here the report of a meeting of the town council of Smiths Falls. Earlier in the session we heard that the district about that town was comparatively well off. Here is the quotation:
.... town council at its regular meeting last night ....
This is dated July 7, 1931.
. . . . heard the startling statement that families in this town were starving and that in some cases were absolutely without provisions. ... In speaking on unemployment conditions, Councillor P. A. McKeown declared that some families in Smiths Falls were "starving" and thought a committee should be appointed to work in connection with church and welfare societies in order to raise a fund to provide relief for the families of unemployed during the coming winter.

Farm and Unemployment Relief
"There have been cases," he said "where families were absolutely without provisions for the week end. They have come to me on Saturday nights and I have had to go out and dig up enough food to carry them over the week end."
Returning to the situation in my own constituency for a moment, I crave the attention of the Prime Minister to the last report of the welfare board which was appointed there. Let me briefly state that the situation became so desperate towards last spring that a meeting was called of the church authorities, the civic authorities and other influential persons in Drumheller, and at that meeting it was decided to set up a local relief board. This was done. That relief board functioned as long as all the funds the town council thought they could possibly vote lasted. Recently the resources being exhausted, even the official relief officer has gone, and the only body dealing with the situation there is a voluntary body created by some warm hearted Canadians who are doing their best to carry on the work formerly done by the relief board. This is the quotation I wish to read:
"We only have a small supply of tea and some dry bread," said a lady asking Mrs. L. Maekay, local relief officer, for relief early this week. "My husband is laid off from the mine permanently (at least until next fall) and we' have no hopes for the future." This is only one of the many pitiful talcs heard daily at the relief office.
Another case is that of a destitute family who could not send their children to school because of lack of footwear. There are four children in the family, the youngest four years old. Since the welfare board has stepped in to help, the three children going to school have been provided with shoes and the younger one, who can only stand at the door and watch the other children play, will be -provided with shoes as soon as further donations are made to the welfare board.
In some eases there are six children in the family and the board is supplying these with milk in an endeavour to restore health and strength to the little bodies.
Donations of money and clothing are needed by the board to continue the work. Mrs. Maekay is always busy investigating cases, and so far as can be learned very few undeserving cases are slipping by. If any of our readers can spare a used suit, shoes, or any kind of wearing apparel the same would be gratefully received at the local relief office, upstairs in the city hall.
These, Mr. Speaker, will give this house some conception of conditions with which we are not all closely familiar. The situation is more terrible than anything that has already been said. Now I give to the house an editorial written by a man of whom the Prime Minister knows well, a man held in high esteem in the city of Edmonton. I refer
to Mr. Elmer Roper, editor of the Labour News, who says:
I have something to get off my chest this week. Sunday I had a talk with Mr. Edward-son, the director of Hope Mission in Edmonton, and Monday morning I spent some time with him again, during which I saw the unemployed single men getting their porridge. About a thousand men are being fed in that way, and twenty-five hundred to three thousand bowls of porridge are being ladled out each day. The place opens xip at seven-thirty and stays open until eleven in the morning, then opens again at three, and mush is dispensed until seven. The most striking thing about the whole business, to me, is the ages of the men. They range, I should say, from twenty to thirty. There is only a sprinkling of older men. Another noticeable feature is the cleanliness of most of them, and the fact that the majority whom I saw seem to be English-speaking fellows. I came away with a deep sense of the tragedy of the whole affair. With a few noticeable exceptions, they were a fine looking group of young men. (They'd have made wonderful recruits in the war). _ They possess the potentialities of good service to society. But because of society's lack of intelligence they are being demoralized and their energies are being wasted.
, That is the situation, Mr. Speaker. Due to the delay all summer long countless thousands, nay, tens of thousands of single unemployed men have drifted across this country from city to city in misery; almost hopeless; begging; living at missions; sleeping where they can; riding on freight trains; learning how to steal; learning how to beg; learning how to starve. What an indictment of a country rich beyond the dreams of nations; what an indictment of a government that pledged itself to solve the problem; what an indictment of a nation that prides itself on its vast wealth as well as its potentialities.
If you want the final word, Mr. Speaker, it is to be found in the letters I have received from those who beg to be deported. We have heard much in this house from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others against the policy of deportation for certain reasons. I have no particular complaint; so far nothing has come to my attention in that regard. But I have this complaint:	We have a situation here under
which, having invited Britishers to Canada, and having promised them steady work at good wages, we now find the same Britishers failing to get the promised work begging to be deported. Not only that, but they thank you when you secure deportation for them.
I have a letter here from a man named Joe Lewis, a Welshman, who says:
I came out here two years ago from Aberavon, South Wales. M.v wife has been sick ever since, and last February applied for deportation. I have been interviewed by the officer, and this I know is hard to ask you but could



Farm and Unemployment Reliej
you ginger them up that end so as to get the family back home out of this misery? With all fraternal greetings,
I hope to remain,
Fraternally yours,
Joe Lewis.
I think that man now is on his way home. I have another letter here from Wayne, Alberta, written by another Britisher, George Ritchie. I helped secure deportation for him and his family, and he writes as follows:
Well, Mr. Garland, I humbly beg to thank you on behalf of myself and family for the way you handled my case and the trouble and pains you used to help me in my great difficulty of getting away. Needless to say my wife has improved in health already, and looking forward to getting back home.
This country must learn to offer more to its people than the hopelessness depicted in letters of that kind, which have been received not only by myself, but I presume by other members as well. The situation is now in the hands of the Prime Minister; whether we will or not he is going to take to himself power to deal with unemployment in the widest and most drastic fashion. The responsibility for failure will be upon him, but in conclusion I say to him that he will have been derelict in his duty and will have betrayed the best interests of Canada if he permits, so long as he is Prime Minister with the power to vote money, any man or woman to exist on $1.50 per week, or 25 cents per child. If he is not able to provide useful and remunerative work I say at least he should provide these people with enough to supply them with three meals a day, a bed and necessary clothing.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext:
I wish to make a few remarks on this very important resolution. I have always regarded the unemployment question as being the very centre of the great problem of our modern world, the problem that has yet to be solved. We may regard the problem of civilization as being focussed in this unemployment question with which Canada, like all other countries in the world, is confronted to-day.

The resolution before the house recognizes the necessity of giving some relief to the unemployed of our country and it makes a definite proposal as to how this is to be done, seeking from this house the necessary authority to enable the government to carry into effect the policy indicated in the motion.
I look upon that, in itself, as a real step forward. I am quite sure' that the people of Canada will feel relieved when they read the resolution; and they will be more satisfied when they read the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to-day, when he said most definitely that no one was to be hungry or cold or in dire distress in Canada in the coming year, who was willing to work if work could be found. And the right hon. gentleman intimated that where people could not work, or where it was impossible to get work for them, they would be similarly taken care of.
That, to my mind, is the announcement of a policy from which no government in the future will ever be able to depart until the problem of unemployment has been solved. I do not think it has ever been so clearly stated by any government before, that the people of the country should be protected from hunger and cold. And when we realize . that the country itself is well able to meet the situation; when we realize that there is no richer country in the world, certainly not in proportion to population; when we realize that there is an abundance of all kinds of goods which the people require, then we can see that it is only a matter of ordinary common sense and wisdom for a government to declare that it will see to it that the people shall not suffer from any lack of food and clothing.
In this resolution the government undertakes to do what the capitalistic system has failed to do. Whether capitalism will undergo some modification in the future and continue, I do not know. But I do know, as everyone else knows, that it has fallen down; it is not able to distribute to the people who require them the goods which it has produced. Here the government of Canada has definitely undertaken that in the coming year goods will be distributed to the people, at least to such an extent as will prevent hunger and cold.
Now, the question i.s whether or not the policy of the government in this regard is the best one to follow. The Prime Minister has challenged the commoners, if the proposed method is not satisfactory, to suggest a better way of going about it. The criticism so far has been against a request from the

Farm and Unemployment Relief
government for a 'blank cheque from parliament as it has been described. The government is criticized for asking authority to spend as much money as it may see fit, and the Prime Minister has declared that a limitation is undesirable. He asks us-How can it otherwise be done-I do noH think it can be done otherwise with efficiency, nor do I think that if another way could be found it would be wise to take it. I think the proposed method is the wisest under the circumstances. And I have not been converted to that view by the resolution itself nor by the arguments in its defence; for I said the same thing when addressing myself to the unemployment question in the budget debate. At that time the government was criticized for failure to state in the budget a specific amount to be expended in unemployment relief. During that debate I said as clearly as I could that in my opinion the budget was not the place in which to make that provision. I did not think that the government was in a position to say definitely how much was required, and therefore, in taking the same view now, I am not admitting that I have changed my mind in consequence of the resolution. I recognize, in view of all the circumstances, the wisdom of the policy now proposed.
If the government did fix a figure it would be immediately open to criticism that that figure was either too small or too large; some would take one view and some the other. And if a specific sum were indicated, it could be at best only a guess. Moreover, all the municipalities and the provinces would be immediately trying to get their share of what there was, and to get it as quickly as they could. If the appropriation were a large one, chey would be competing with one another to see who could get the most. They would argue, as I have often heard them argue, "We have to pay for it anyway out of our taxes and we may as well get as much as we possibly can." Another consideration is this. If a specific sum were mentioned the tendency of the manufacturers and large employers of labour would be to rest on their oars more or less. They would feel that they had less responsibility than 'before in our present industrial situation, because the government had decided to spend so much to relieve unemployment.
Taking all phases of the question into consideration, I am quite satisfied that the government could not declare what specific amount would be required. They could only guess at it, and even if they were approximately right it would not be good policy. It is far better for us to give the government
what it now asks, namely, the right to expend whatever sum is necessary and where it is necessary. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we must entrust any government, under circumstances such as we are faced with now, with that much authority. The government in accepting responsibility in this regard, cannot, if it fails, escape its responsibility to the people; if it misspends the money or if its policy proves to be a fiasco, parliament and the people will have to deal with the subject again. The government cannot escape its responsibility in this regard even if it were desirous of so doing. We are now taking the logical and wisest step in order to deal with a specific situation.
It has been contended, especially by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), that the government by this measure is being granted too much power. I am not sure that I can quite follow the logic of that argument. According to our system the government. for all practical purposes, is parliament, and parliament is the government. I would say that the objection that, the government is getting too much power under this bill has not even a technical basis upon which to rest, for the government makes its appeal to parliament and parliament is the majority of this house. The majority of the house belongs to the government side, and the government controls the party in power. Therefore, in reality, in respect to not only this government but all governments under the party system, the government is parliament and parliament is the government. Theoretically we can argue otherwise if we choose to do so; theoretically we can say that parliament has this, that and the other thing, but the only thing that parliament has is the decision of the majority. The decision of the majority is that of the government party in every case, and the government party is controlled very largely by the cabinet. Perhaps this is a good thing in most instances. There you have the situation, so what is the use of saying that parliament is now being ravished and the government is obtaining powers greater than it has any right to receive? Under our system the government cannot do that if it brings the measure to the house, for it is parliament that is now acting. In that regard I could not follow the reasoning of my good friend and colleague, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), when he stated that the government under this bill was usurping the power of parliament. I am at a loss to see how parliament can usurp the power of parliament; for, I repeat, this bill will have to be passed by the majority of this house which

Farm and Unemployment Relief
is the voice of parliament, and parliament cannot usurp its own powers. As a matter of fact, this bill does not seek power; it expresses power, and anyone who wishes to challenge that statement must challenge our entire system of government. I have done that many a time, and I still do it. I do not think this is the best system of government, but it is the system that exists and in this bill the government is carrying out the constitutional method. There is nothing wrong with that. Anyone who criticizes it ought to challenge the system itself, because that is the only ground he would have in this connection.
To pass on to the other phase of the question which has been touched upon by the Prime Minister and those who replied to him, in regard to the powers whereby the government seeks to enforce law and order, any government must be clothed with powers to act in an emergency in order to protect the system for which it stands. That is a principle which cannot be put aside even though we may not be supporters of the government or of the order of society which it represents. The power to meet any emergency is inseparable from the idea of government; it is inherent in government. A government without power to protect itself is not a government at all. I do not know that Canada is in any great danger of revolutionary uprising at present; I would say that probably it is in less danger in that respect than any other country in the world, but I know as well as any other hon. member that there are those Who seek to upset by force this system, not only in this country but in all others, and they do not hesitate to say so. They declare that all governments exist by force, which is true, and they say that we can upset that government or system only by force. They openly say: We are out by force to upset that system. They know quite well that power of this kind is inherent in government and they do not hesitate so to declare. I do not know to what extent the danger may be from that quarter; I think it is very small; but if there were a danger I would not want to accept the responsibility of not having provision made to take care of it. When there are numbers of people in the country who openly declare they are out to upset the Whole system by force, I do not consider that method intelligent, and I am still trying to hold on to my faith in the possibility of modifying our present system through intelligence. While I do not agree with the system as it exists to-day; while I have every hope that a new system will be established, nevertheless I can

see that if the system as it is were swept away by those who would seek to detroy it, I would be defeated in trying to modify the system through intelligence just as those who believe in the system would be defeated. To that exent there is no middle course: we must either openly and avowedly take our side with those who stand for the overthrow of the system by force, or else give our support both moral and direct to the protection of the system at it exists. Therefore, I see no objection to giving the government the authority which it asks. Even if there is no danger of their having to use it, the government must be clothed with that authority.
I hope the clothes will fit well; if they do not, the government will have to pay for the misfit.	_ ,
I would deplore nothing more than civil disruption to any degree in Canada next year or any other year; I would deplore that there should be any act which would warrant the government in exercising that power, but-it would be equally deplorable if conditions arose which demand its exercise and the government did not have the right to use it. So from that point of view I see no reason why this measure Should not be passed.
Let me turn next to the main proposal, and the one in which we are all more interested than even in these points of academic discussion. I refer to the question of how to meet the unemployment situation that at present exists in Canada. Of course I know the government, in taking this course, does not consider it is solving the problem of unemployment for all time. It will give employment to the people only while they are doing the work which is provided for them, and not any longer. There is nothing in the proposal that would indicate a fundamental alteration in the system itself that would do away with unemployment. But the action that is being taken is very necessary at the present time, and the question is: what suggestions can we make to the government in this regard?
I was glad indeed to hear the declaration that the government intended to enter upon extensive public works, to provide constructive. real work, not work that is manufactured by groups and municipalities as is sometimes done, merely to keep idle hands busy, like carrying a heavy stone from one end of the garden to the other for eight hours a day in order that a man may feel morally justified that he had done sufficient work to entitle him to eat three meals. That kind of work we do not want, but real constructive work which is required, work which will be an asset

Farm and Unemployment Relief
to the nation, work which will assist Canada to produce greater wealth in the future than it has in the past. That is the kind of work we desire to have done, and I am delighted that the government has seen fit to announce that policy now because I believe that that in itself is a mark of progress.
As I have perhaps too often said to this house in criticism of government policies generally in respect to unemployment, most governments during times of depression spend less money than at any other time, and most governments during times of great prosperity have a tendency to spend more money than at any other time. That is the natural reaction. I say, to the general public feeling, but I argue that it is bad policy. The governments of the country, municipal, provincial and dominion, taken together represent a greater control of the capital expenditure of this country than any other force, and if all these governments would undertake to plan carefully even their own expenditure, they could to a very great extent regulate the periods of depression and unemployment. They have control. They may spend this year or next year. I think that the adoption of such a policy by the government would be a step in advance; not that it would cure anything, but it might prevent a good deal of unnecessary suffering if all the governments of Canada, municipal, provincial and dominion, would undertake to think ahead and to engage in capital expenditure to the greatest extent in times of depression and to husband its resources in times of prosperity. That would have a regulating effect upon the boom and slump cycles which unfortunately come because we have not intelligent control of finance in relation to production and distribution.
There are many kinds of work which the government could undertake, and may I suggest that the government ought to do this thing in a big way if it is going to do it at all. I hope the government will do it in such a way that it will not be necessary for working people to lower their standard of living next winter. I hope that they will engage in it in such a way that it will not be necessary to reduce wages below the ordinary standards, and that they will engage in it in a big enough way to give a stimulus to the whole business life of Canada. It may not take so much to do that as we might at first think. Unquestionably the depression in this and all other countries is due to the fact that there is not sufficient purchasing power amongst the people to distribute the goods the production of which the modern machine
has made possible. You may explain that any way you like. But put the money into the pockets of the people of Canada to-day and you will not require any money for unemployment relief. There would be plenty to do. You would then have the purchasing power necessary to move the goods now lying on the dust-laden shelves of the warehouses, and as soon as those goods are moved the wheels of industry will start replenishing the shelves, and then you are off. The great question is to distribute purchasing power, and I hope the government will enter into this building of public service in such a way as to make a real impression on the economic life of the country. There are so many things that might Ire done. I shall enumerate a few of the smaller ones first, and then finish up with a few of the larger ones.
There could be built schools and colleges. We need more of both. Roads and bridges could be built. Electric and Steam railways, footpaths, parks, the making of improvements, such as pavements and so forth, the building of hospitals, sanatoria and laboratories, public buildings, the improvement of harbours, the development of canals and generally the means of inland navigation, the reclamation of waste lands, reforestation, the making of supplies for public institutions, such as clothing, uniforms and furniture.
May I add to that list, the building of houses for the people of Canada to live in? There is not one of our large cities in Canada, so far as I am aware, which has escaped the slum condition characteristic of older cities. Go to Montreal or Toronto, or even to Winnipeg, and you will find street after street of houses that ought to be burned down. You will find people struggling to pay high rents for houses because houses are scarce. At the same time you will find hundreds of idle carpenters, hundreds of idle plumbers, hundreds of men idle who would like to dig cellars and make concrete basements. You will find lumber burning up in the sun in the lumber yards of Canada, and tall timber in the forests waiting to be cut down with the axe. We have all these things in abundance, and yet we have people without houses to live in. Go on the prairies among the farmers and you will find dozens of farmers living in hovels, shacks, with t'he rain pouring in on them when it rains, and the occupants freezing almost to death in the winter time. These people require better houses, and it would be in the interest of Canada to build them. It is far better for us to build houses, to remove the slums from our cities, to raise the standard of living for our agriculturists,

Farm and Unemployment Relief
than merely to give hand-outs in relief in order to keep people from starving. Such is the kind of constructive work that I hope the government will undertake.
Let me now indicate a few things that might be done in a bigger way. We hope that some day in the near future the deep waterway on the St. Lawrence will be developed. We hope that in the near future it will be possible to travel by motor from the eastern coast to the western coast. We want that highway built, whether it is built as a national highway all the way through or the stretches of provincial highways are merely linked up. That work should be done. It would be of great service to the people of Canada. To give another example, take the Peace River outlet, which has already been mentioned by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). There is a necessary railway to be built; the people are needing it, and there cannot be a more advantageous time to build it than now when money can be borrowed perhaps more cheaply than in the midst of a period of prosperity. There are three great undertakings. Let them be undertaken as speedily as possible, as well as similar undertakings. Suppose it puts Canada $500,000,000 more in debt. Suppose it even went so far as to put Canada 81,000.000.000 more in debt, for construction, for peace, for the development of national life, a billion dollars in the interests of constructive human" statesmanship. Suppose it did. Could not that well be defended? We cannot defend the expenditure of two billion dollars for war. I do not know of anybody who either then or now would say that we could have got rid of that expenditure, but after all, what have we to show for it but thousands of graves of our best in Flanders, hundreds and thousands of our citizens crippled, and all the ill-feeling which develops as the result of a world war of that magnitude, with all the problems which have been created thereby? And still we have to meet all the little wars and all the big wars which the peace following the last war made possible. That is all we got, out of it. All the goods were produced and destroyed, but for a peace program of this kind the goods we produce will remain to reproduce themselves in the greater wealth of the nation. I do not think any government has to fear criticism from intelligent people when they undertake the expenditures necessary to meet the country's needs in the midst of an economic breakdown of society such as is common to all nations of the world to-day. The government has committed itself to a policy of protecting Canadian citizens from hunger and starvation,

and it proposes to do so, not merely by doling out a few dollars -now and again, but by constructive work. I have tried to indicate some of 'the things I believe should be done under that .program by the municipal and provincial governments in joint operation with the federal government.
The question now arises:	Where is the
money to come from to carry out these works? That is the greatest problem which any government of to-day has to face. I do not know whether the government has agreed with what I have said so far, but I am sorry to say I am sure it will not agree with my next statements. From now on I go alone, so far as the government is concerned. The government does not believe it is possible to finance our national undertakings in any way other than the method which in the past has been adopted. I am quite convinced that the day is not far distant when this or some other government wlil change its mind on that point. Throughout the entire world the question of credit is to-day the chief matter of discussion. We know that at the moment Europe is almost at the point of breakdown, through lack of proper credit facilities. We know that condition has been brought about by a debt creating system which, by its very nature, grows from day to day and from generation to generation until the burden of the world's debt becomes so terrific that the financial structure crumbles under the weight. To put it another way, international and national debts have so absorbed the credit of the people that there is nothing left to live on, and nothing left to circulate or to make goods move. There is nothing left with which to enter into new productions, so great has become the debt system. If we proceed with a program such as that indicated in the resolution we shall have to borrow or create money to do it. If we borrow the money, the banks create it; if we create it, we do ourselves what the banks would do for us. That is the only difference.
I am going to suggest, as I have done ad nauseam to this house, that the government consider the possiblity of financing this matter by putting the national credit behind it, and not by issuing debt and interest bearing bonds which will not only add to the debt but in twenty years will be doubled, and will add to the burden of debt from which the nations of the world are at the present time struggling to free themselves. I do not suppose it would be edifying to hon. members if I were to attempt to analyze the credit system of Canada. I do not think I would be justified in letting this opportun-

Farm and Unemployment Relief
ity pass, however, without emphasizing that this is a time when an experiment could be made, at least on a small scale. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) has been urging that we should alter the gold basis of our currency sufficiently to place us on a par with countries with whom we have to compete in business. Here is a method of achieving that result without doing anything with the gold. Let there be issued in Canada sufficient credit to undertake these public services, and immediately, as the Prime Minister will declare, if asked, currency will be debased to correspond with the currency of other countries, and immediately we shall have done what the hon. member for Macleod has been asking us to do and would place ourselves on a level with Australia, Argentine and the countries with which we must compete when selling our goods in the markets of the world. They would not have an advantage, as they do now, of between 25 and 30 per cent when they sell their goods to countries to which we desire also to sell.
I do not think I could add much more to the discussion. That the government has undertaken to deal with the problem of unemployment is a mark of progress. I believe it should be a part of the government's policy to regulate its public works with a view to doing most of them at a time when we have greatest unemployment, and doing least when we have greater prosperity. Further, I believe that the financing of such an undertaking should be done directly from the treasury of the state without any interest charges beyond those which are necessary to meet the handling charges. In that way we would increase the purchasing power of the community without increasing its debt, and by increasing the purchasing power we would stimulate industry in Canada and go a long way towards relieving the present unemployment situation.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. W. KENNEDY (Winnipeg South Centre):
subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the city of Winnipeg is vitally concerned in the measure of relief foreshadowed by this resolution. In point of population Winnipeg is the third city in Canada; in normal times it is the third city in point of the value of its industrial output. To-day Winnipeg stands first among the cities of Canada in the gravity of the unemployment situation; surely that is a matter of real concern. I think I am not overstating the facts when I say that in that city and its immediate environs there are to-day 30,000 workless. Who are those workless people? Many, it is true, are transients; many are unskilled workmen; many,
too, are skilled artisans; there are clerks and divers other classes of citizens who in times of normal prosperity administer to the multitudinous needs of a great metropolis.
It is my privilege to represent in this house an important constituency in that city, that of Winnipeg South Centre. That constituency, including that portion of the municipality of St. James immediately adjoining on the west, contains, conservatively speaking, about 125,000 people. Its aotual voting strength at the last general election was approximately 47,000. In it there are all classes of people living under normal standards. There are people of moderate wealth, but the vast majority are engaged in business, in retail trades, in various working and building trades; some are clerks-indeed I think I may describe the constituency as one representative of the working people of Canada who depend upon their day's work for their daily bread.
It has been intimated in the press throughout the country that Winnipeg of all the cities of Canada is a city where there congregate in large numbers those who for want of a more accurate description the papers call "reds." I am here to-night, sir, to say that that is untrue. The vast majority of the people of the city of Winnipeg, as I believe of all other cities in this country, call them what you like, are plain, honest citizens, seeking only the right to work and to maintain their families in reasonable comfort. It is true that in Winnipeg, as in other cities, we have certain professional agitators whose dividends depend upon dissension, discord and agitation. But, thank God, they are few. While they are articulate and vociferous, and consequently acquire a notoriety and a publicity far beyond their numerical importance, let me say that at heart the city of Winnipeg is sound. In fifty years it has' grown from a hamlet to be the third city of Canada; I am proud to-night to be a representative from that city.
The people of Winnipeg-and may I presume to speak not merely for the people of my constituency, but for the fair-minded people of Winnipeg, generally-are looking with hope to the legislation that is at present before this house. I am happy to say that I think they have reason to look with hope, indeed to look with far greater hope than would be indicated by the criticism offered by the ex-Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon and by those who have followed him in a similar vein. Since I have referred to the ex-Prime Minister, I think I could not better describe the plight

Farm and Unemployment Relief
of these people than to use his own language in his book on Industry and Humanity. At page 51 in discussing people in like circumstances he says:
The sufferings of the victims of economic pressure are not so dramatically displayed as are the sacrifices of men in war. They are none the less real, though being silently, slowly and obscurely borne.
That is true, sir-it is comparatively easy, booted and spurred, with bugles calling to ride into action with death tugging at your stirrup leathers; but to be denied the right to earn your daily bread, to sit without employment, hope or aim by an unlighted hearth, to watch your children, your dependents in hunger and in want-that is something that plumbs the greatest depths of human fortitude. That is the plight to-night of these
30,000	people in the city of Winnipeg. I hope, sir, that this house will not consider I am parochial in referring only to the city of Winnipeg. I refer to Winnipeg because it is my city, and I think it is consistent with the duty of every member on an occasion such as this to concern himself particularly with the needs of his own constituency. I realize that similar conditions exist, not to that extent perhaps, but to whatever extent they do exist in other part3 of Canada they are equally critical. For that reason I am glad to know that when parliament prorogues I can go back to the city of Winnipeg, knowing that the Prime Minister and his cabinet have seen fit to place, as they will place, upon the statute books an instrument by which the government during the long winter months that are to come will be in a position to deal effectively and adequately with the crisis that is upon ua
To ameliorate these conditions is, and should be, the first duty of government. Ha3 this government recognized its duty? The matter need not be extended. Let me simply say this: The Conservative party, led by the Right Hon. Richard B. Bennett, in the campaign just closed a year ago yesterday, told the people of Canada that when our citizens :ould not find work in a land of plenty, when they were denied the right to work, that was a matter of national concern. He told the people of Canada that if the Conservative party were returned to power it would recognize unemployment as a national problem and would so deal with it. A special session was called; that w'as the first step in fulfilment of the promise. Following that there was initiated in this house-however it may turn out eventually-a policy which in the judgment of the government of the day is predicated upon this principle: That Canadian workmen in Canada shall have the right, as

far as is economically possible, to work up into the finished product the goods that will be consumed in this country. That is the principle upon which this government is proceeding with a view to bringing about permanent amelioration of general conditions. But in the meantime, since we have unemployment slill with us, there will be introduced now a measure to provide for the immediate circumstances.
It is rather surprising to me as a comparatively new member in this house to find that members opposite seek always apparently only something to condemn, nothing to commend. It has come as a surprise to me that those who claim to represent labour in a special sense could find so little to commend in the legislation now before the house. I am glad the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) is in his place, because I want to make a brief reference to his criticism. Read the speech of the hon. member and recall that it is relative to a resolution recognizing unemployment as a matter of first national concern, that asks this house to place in the hands of the government an instrument whereby it can adequately cope with the situation as it arises. Yet how little of commendation is to be found in the hon member's remarks. There may have been a phrase of commendation-if there was I missed it-but I did not miss the carping, factious criticism. The hon. member charged-what? That this government seeks autocratic powers. Autrocratic powers, forsooth! What are they? The government of the day seeks only this right: the authority of parliament to work out in cooperation with the municipalities and the provinces a measure of relief for our own workless, and to that end to use such funds of this country' as the occasion warrants. Autocratic powers! The scope of the request is measured by the need, and by the need alone That far, and no further, the government seeks authority from this parliament.
The hon. member found occasion too to refer to newspaper despatches relating to alleged statements by the Hon. Mr. Finlayson of the Ontario government, intimating what was likely to happen in certain camps in the north of the province. So far, so good. But not until his attention was definitely directed to it by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) did he say, "Yes I did read denials by Mr. Finlayson." Is it too much to expect, sir, that one who in former years was engaged in the promulgation of the principle, "do unto others as you would they should do unto you," would be fair enough in the first instance to place the two statements side by side?

Farm and Unemployment Reliej
The hon. member also seems to fear that some sinister use is intended to be made by this government of the special powers asked for looking to the preservation of peace, order and good government in this country. Does any fair-minded man throughout the whole of Canada believe that either the right hon. Prime Minister or any member of his cabinet really seeks that power for any ulterior or sinister purpose? I am sure there is not one. Who are apprehensive? Only those who have cause. Let me remind the hon. member of a text with which I am sure he will be familiar: The guilty flee when no man pursueth.
Reference was made also, Mr. Speaker, by the same hon. member to the first citizen of the city of Winnipeg. I hold no brief for Colonel Ralph Webb, mayor of the city of Winnipeg; he does not need me to tell the people of Canada where he stands, but coming from that city I felt I could not let the observation pass. When speaking of deportations it was suggested by the hon. member that the first deportee be Ralph Webb. Let me say that if we deported from Canada every citizen of the type of Ralph Webb of r.he city of Winnipeg, and left only citizens of the communistic type who want to subvert our constitution and all our principles of liberty, Canada indeed would be a very bad country in which to dwell.
The right hon. the ex-Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) devoted his whole speech to criticism, and without going into detail I took this to be his major criticism: He intimated that by giving this government power to draw upon the resources of this country without limitation, for unemployment relief, we would be doing violence to the constitution of Canada and abrogating the powers and privileges of parliament. He contended that something in the proposal was fundamentally wrong, and that in asking parliament to grant this power we were shattering precedent. Sir, how often in the past has the Conservative party in Canada had to listen to the taunt that they were a party of reactionaries, fettered by precedent and afraid to move without some precedent to back up that movement? It is a happy change, then, for those who have been accustomed to indulge in those taunts to have this outstanding example to the contrary to meet a national crisis. If it be-and I do not think it is-that we are asking parliament to stretch a little the garment with which the constitution of Canada is clothed, then never before in the history of Canada was there such warrant and such merit for the request. Although the ex-Prime Minister may be disturbed by the shattering of this precedent; although some of the others who followed him in like strain may be disturbed, let me
say that I think the people of Canada are not particularly concerned whether we stretch that garment an inch or more. But they are concerned with this government dealing in an adequate and courageous way with the problem now preeminently occupying the minds of the people.
At the most it is this: Parliament is asked to trust this administration, in dealing with this matter of unemployment, not to squander the money of the people. Shortly, that is all there is to it. The ex-Prime Minister says we should fix the sum, that it should be limited. What sum could be fixed, with conditions changing from day to day? Who in April last, by the utmost prevision, could have foreseen that in the great province of Saskatchewan there would be an area of some five million acres practically without a crop? Who could have foreseen that situation? Now we know it to be so. The ex-Prime Minister says this legislation should have been brought in at the commencement of the session; had that been done there would have been no relief for the cropless farmers in the west.
During this whole summer the Department of Labour has been in touch with the situation and has been gathering information, and I submit that now is the most opportune time to deal with this question. Just as conditions changed fundamentally from what they were in May last, so in October, November and December they may vary again. Then what sum can be asked of this parliament for this purpose? A maximum could be fixed, but if that were not enough what would happen then? It is a matter of trusting this administration to act judiciously as trustees of the funds of the people in order adequately to meet the situation as it arises, and as it varies from time to time. If that is too much it means that this house cannot trust the present administration. Happily the people of Canada have seen fit to trust them, and it is my belief that this whole question of unemployment will be so met and dealt with that the government will continue to merit the confidence of the people.
Just one further word and I am through. The ex-Prime Minister is now very much disturbed about our workless. Is it too much to expect that our unemployed will measure the magnanimity of his present concern when he has not the power to execute, by the parsimony of his performance when he had the power to help?
