This robust New Brunswick red herring having been drawn across the trail, perhaps now we may have a chance to come back to the very important question before the house. It seems to me that in these last days of the session, with everyone anxious to see the session concluded, hon. members are apt to minimize the importance of the proposition before us. We should distinguish quite clearly between the object in view, the policy propounded by the government in order to attain that object, and the means chosen to give effect to that policy.
As far as the object to be reached is concerned I think no one disagrees; everyone admits that a very grave crisis is upon us, and I do not think any useful purpose would be served by rehashing the arguments which took place during the last election. The Conservatives, perhaps not without reason, condemned the Liberals for not having grasped the situation fully before the election, while on the other hand the Conservatives themselves committed the fault of making promises which I do not say they knew then but which they realize now could not be fully implemented. No doubt a great deal of the moral disquietude and the somewhat bitter feeling which have grown up in the country arise largely from the fact that the people, not seeing the immediate fulfilment of promises which could not be immediately implemented, are apt to take a rather wrong view of the situation and of the government. For my part I feel quite at ease, because, having nothing to do with either party during the last election, I could say quite plainly to the people whose confidence I enjoy that whatever party came into power the crisis was bound to be worse the year following and for perhaps another year, whatever policy was adopted. Knowing a little of the conditions of the world as they were; knowing that the deep causes of that crisis went far back into the past and that most of the apparent prosperity which followed the war was a fake prosperity kept up by a system of credit which could not but fail when the conditions which existed in Europe should

reach us, I felt quite sure that the farmer, the industrialist and the workman had worse days to anticipate, and they have come.
At the special session the government obtained from the house, without much difficulty, permission to spend $20,000,000 under certain conditions. As far as I am concerned I do not blame the government for not having realized that some of the conditions attached to the spending of that money would put many municipalities in a bad position. I cannot blame the government now, because I did not blame them then. I took the view, which was taken by the ex-Prime Minister and I think by the present Prime Minister also at one time, that there was a joint responsibility; that the first responsibility was that of the municipality, then that of the province and finally that of the federal government. Therefore I thought the legislation was proper.
With regard to the amount of money voted, naturally, it was only in the course of the months which followed that the government could realize what further needs would have to be met by parliament; but here the failure of the government begins. It comes about largely, I think, because of that peculiar viewpoint expressed by the Prime Minister this afternoon, when he evidently thought it his duty and the duty of the government to maintain in the country a spirit of optimism. Optimism is a good thing provided it is based on realities; but I do not think enthusiastic optimism is any better than pessimism for the curing of such evils as that with which we must deal. What is needed on the part of statesmen, of men of influence, of everyone who can direct public opinion and manage public affairs, is neither optimism nor pessimism but cool-headed realism, plently of courage to face the situation and also courage to tell the whole truth to the people.
As far as that is concerned I think no one would accuse the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) of lacking in courage, but I am afraid he has failed to speak the whole truth to all classes of the community. No doubt he was more or less tied up by the declarations he made during the campaign; but now, after a year in power, after the experience he had in dealing with the situation last winter, he ought to have put himself, and the members of the government ought to have put themselves, in the position of stating clearly-I will not say in every detail but on broad lines-the policy which they proposed to adopt. This resolution fails to do so. It is all very well to say that these are abnormal circumstances and

that we should not tie up the government by a legal technicality or an article of the constitution, as the eloquent and charming member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy) suggested. We are not concerned with a clause of the constitution in this matter; we are concerned with a fundamental principle of parliamentary government. It is not written in the British North America Act; it is not written in any statute of this land or of the motherland; it is that basic principle that the elementary duty of the representatives of the people is to keep control of all the sums of money gathered from the people by way of taxation, anid to confide to their executive committee such powers as are necessary properly to apply that money derived from the people by taxation, according to the will of parliament. I claim, sir, that we have no right to abdicate a particle of that duty and of that function. It is not a question of trusting or mistrusting this or any other government. It is a question of keeping in their proper order the functions of government and the functions of parliament.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) suggested in passing that this resolution smacked of bolshevism. No; I think he was wrong there. But it does show a strong touch of fascism, undoubtedly. Now, what has substituted fascism for parliamentary government in Italy? I am not criticizing the attitude of the Italian people; they knew their circumstances. And I knew enough of those circumstances to appreciate their position, because I was in Italy in the very year of the advance of the. fascist army; I left Rome a few months before they took possession. Possibly, with conditions as they were in Italy at that time, the only material salvation of the country was the abdication of parliamentary control into the hands of a strong government. But have we come to that in Canada? I do not think that the Prime Minister, in the very plausible speech he made this afternoon, has given a single cogent reason for asking, for the first time in the history of parliamentary government in Canada, that this house should divest itself of a fundamental, I will not say right, but function and duty.
The suggestion has been made that the government cannot very well say precisely what amount is needed. That suggestion came either from the Prime Minister or from some of his followers, and it was repeated even by an over-zealous member in this comer, who in the first thirty minutes of his speech seemed to me to be making a bid to be the first to benefit by the law passed a few days ago to allow

Farm and Unemployment Relief
members to be appointed to the cabinet without re-election. The hon. gentleman seemed better informed of the policy of the government than the Prime Minister himself. But let that pass. It has been said that the circumstances are such that the government cannot state exactly what amount of money they need. But surely that is true of any large enterprise which is subsidized by parliament. When Sir John Macdonald came to parliament and asked for the first subsidy in lands and money to the Canadian Pacific Railway he did not know what that undertaking was going to cost. Indeed, no one knew. But he asked for 25,000,000 acres of land and $25,000,000; and later on various forms of assistance were given. Or let us come to the time when the Meighen administration decided to take over the bankrupt enterprises of Mackenzie and Mann and the Grand Trunk Railway, and when that right hon. gentleman was described by his successor, the present Prime Minister, in rather exaggerated language, as the gramophone of Mackenzie and Mann. The circumstances then were very difficult, and I am not one who blames Mr. Meighen for having done what he did. But he did not know exactly to what he was committing Canada; yet he asked for something precise to start with.
When the war broke out it created an issue as grave, surely, as the present one. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon quoted some of the war measures. At every session of parliament during the war Sir Robert Borden came and asked for so many millions to carry on war operations until the following year. Everyone knew it was not enough; he knew and the opposition knew. But it never entered Sir Robert Borden's head to ask for a blank cheque for the duration of the war. He did not say, "I do not know what it will cost; I do not know what will be the loss in men and money; let parliament abdicate its functions and have confidence in the government".
I have as much confidence in the integrity and ability of the present Prime Minister as I had in the integrity and ability of Sir Robert Borden or of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. But in the old days, under Liberal or Conservative administrations, I did oppose any attempt to increase unduly the powers of the cabinet at the expense of parliament. And to-day I oppose that attempt, remaining true to the principle of parliamentary government.
It is not a question of men; it is not a question of parties; it is not a question of personal trust in this or that man. It is a question of principle. I have stated before, 22110-2744
and I repeat now: If the people of Canada have come to the conclusion that parliamentary government is not the best form of government for our country, it is for them to say. I have already said, and I say again, that I have lost a good deal of my faith in parliamentary government. But so long as we have it we must work it out in the spirit of its fundamental principles * and not encroach upon those principles without realizing what we are doing.
History, and particularly English history, shows that the great danger to popular liberty and to popular representation in times of crisis is twofold. At one extreme there are those who are apt to minimize the gravity of any situation and, so to speak, to tie the hands of government by adhering too rigidly to many legal technicalities which, while necessary under ordinary circumstances, are undesirable in a crisis. At the other extreme there are people who are blinded by the exigencies of a passing situation, and without due reflection, or with a desire to please people by satisfying their immediate material needs, will sacrifice great principles which it has cost centuries of effort to establish. This has been several times exemplified in the history of parliamentary government in Great Britain. At the moment I will refer only to one instance that comes to my mind. At the beginning of the French revolution, a hundred years after the English revolution, and after a long process of liberalizing legislation, religious and social; after all those declarations of right for wffiich men had fought in the hope that succeeding generations would benefit thereby; in the reaction from the French revolution one who was perhaps the greatest English parliamentarian, Edmund Burke, went to the right and Charles Fox to the left. Charles Fox, imbued as he was with the principles of liberty, attempted and to a certain extent succeeded perhaps in shaking the confidence of the English people in its monarchy. But Edmund Burke, that great reformer whose words, uttered in time of calm and peace, will remain forever a source of inspiration to all who believe in English parliamentary government-Edmund Burke, I say, in his dread of French Jacobinism, outdid some of the most rabid English Tories. He went further than the Pitts and those who were then employed in strengthening the hand of the government to combat revolution and to carry on the war on the continent. Surely the situation in Canada to-day is not such that we should lose our heads to the point of abrogating the duties and the functions of parliament.

The Prime Minister has made an allusion rather than a reference to the difficulty in which, perhaps, he has found himself or in which he may find himself in the future, in the apportionment of the amount of money needed as between provinces. I hasten to agree with him that we should at once dispel the idea that may exist right or left, east or west, that. this fund is going to be given to the provinces according to population. Neither the leader of the opposition nor anybody that I have heard has suggested that the government should declare what amount of money they are going to spend in Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan or elsewhere. Nobody could reasonably ask that. Of course, if the situation in Saskatchewan is such that in proportion to population they require to spend in that province twice or three times as much as is needed in Quebec, they are welcome to do so, but that does not change the position with regard to the principle of the resolution. The government could have asked for an amount of 850,000,000 or $75,000,000 or $100,000,000 to be apportioned as between provinces and various works of relief according to circumstances, and I for one, would have ungrudgingly granted the government that power.
I have already touched upon the question of the limitation of the amount by referring to past examples. I consider the argument advanced by the leader of the opposition this afternoon is incontrovertible. The government has the power of calling a session of parliament whenever it is needed. Surely in those twelve months, I khall not say of enjoyment of office, because I know the Prime Minister has not had twelve months of enjoyment; but in those twelve months of fulfilment of his duty-and I give him this credit, that he has done perhaps more than he should have done personally in the accomplishment of his duty-he has gathered sufficient information to be in a position to state to parliament that in order to carry on this work of relief until the month of January next, a certain sum of money will be required, just as on the 18th day of August, 1914, Sir Robert Borden was capable of stating to the House of Commons what amount of money was needed to commence the work of the war. The positions are the same; the principles are alike; and I see no reason why we should change them now.
I do not want to dwell at any greater length upon this broad aspect of the situation, but as one of the oldest members of the house I appeal to every hon. member, to whatever party he belongs, to think twice before he

sets aside those great principles of parliamentary government. It is all very well to unfold the British flag and to sing the National Anthem upon all occasions; but there is a more effective way of showing that we are attached, not to the person of a king, not to the emblem of a form of government, but to the principles of a system that has done more to unite the various races and classes of Canada into one contented nation than anything else could have done.
With regard to the application, again I agree entirely with the leader of the opposition. I see no reason why the government should not have asked first for the right to come to the relief of the unemployed and, as a means to accomplish that object, to help the provinces and the municipalities. Then they could have brought in a special measure for farm relief. ' As a matter of fact, I think it would have been far better to have those two measures separate, in order to define precisely the powers of the government. We shall see, of course, by the bill to what extent this separation is accomplished, and therefore I shall not dilate any longer upon this point. I wish simply to answer the argument of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, who said that in the month of April the situation in Saskatchewan could not have been foreseen. If the government had done in this instance as they did in every other; if they had treated each subject on its merits, they could have been in a position on the 12th day of March to forecast in the speech from the throne what they proposed to do with regard to unemployment which has been upon us for at least the last two years. Later on they could have come in with a measure regarding Saskatchewan. But to take the situation in Saskatchewan in May and June to excuse the government for proposing nothing to the house and the country prior to the last days of the session, to settle another problem which was just as acute in March as it is now, which, in fact, was just as acute in January as it was in March, is no explanation or excuse that can be reasoned out.
With regard to the application, leaving aside the question of Saskatchewan which is one by itself, let me assure my hon. friends opposite that, whether they believe it or not, I am speaking in the most disinterested spirit. It is true there is bad feeling as between east and west and as between provinces. This is due to many causes, but let us be frank about the matter. It is due largely as regards the province of Quebec to the campaign which was carried on during the last election.

The work should be apportioned according to the number of members of the family. If in a family of ten two are capable of working, let those two work. If in a family of five, two are capable of working, let one work so as to give the two families an equal chance. That is a matter to be adjusted by the municipality. As far as the boys are concerned, familiar with the surroundings in Montreal or the province, and the same will apply to every large city and to every province, try to give them work not too far away from their centre.
But where the duty of the government is more complicated, and where I think the exclusive duty of the federal government comes in, is in dealing with the foreign transient. I agree with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre that we should not let grow up on the part of the native-born Canadian a feeling of animosity against foreigners. I opposed the immigration policy of the Liberal party for twenty-five years, and therefore I am free to speak on this question. But we now have these foreigners here, some for five years, some for ten years. Even if they have been here only three months, they are human beings just the same; are we going to let them die because they do not speak English or French or because they may be orthodox Russians or Roumanians? No. We have a social and a national and an international duty, as well as a human and a Christian duty, to perform towards them, and I consider that the federal government is the proper authority to look after these people. As was stated

by Mr. Brierley-I do not know what his politics are, but he is a very good social worker in Montreal-we should consider these foreigners as the wards of the nation. Where do they belong to? I do not know. Some have come to Montreal from Saskatchewan, some from Alberta, some from British Columbia. It has been suggested that they be repatriated. The municipal council of Montreal adopted unanimously a resolution to that effect at the suggestion of one of the Jewish representatives there. But there are two sides to that question. If we should repatriate these foreigners on a voluntary basis, the best of them physically, the best socially and the best morally would jump at the chance, just as the two did who were mentioned by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), and we should be left with the dregs. Therefore I am not quite sure that to announce a policy of repatriation is quite the proper thing. I think the government should keep itself absolutely free to deport those who are really undesirable, with due equity, of course, and perhaps to repatriate some. But if we want to accomplish that, we need, first, to develop in each province a sense of responsibility towards the Canadians who have gone from one province to another. Taking into account, however, conditions in our country, politically, socially and otherwise, the problem should be considered as a provincial and municipal matter as well, but we should insist that the city of Montreal or the city of Edmonton, as the case may be, are Canadian cities and are not states within the state. Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few words along lines somewhat different from those thus far pursued. It is not my intention to speak to those phases of the matter which may be regarded as controversial. There was one word in the Prime Minister's speech that claimed my attention, because for the last three or four weeks, in fact for months, it had been on my mind; I refer to the word "cooperation". The necessity for cooperation not only between parties in this house but among all elements in Canada is apparent. When we were face to face with
the war there was a wonderful example of cooperation among the different classes of Canadian people. We sent our soldiers to the front and many of us at home who could not go did the best we could to support our soldiers. We experienced, in a large degree, the spirit of self-sacrifice. At the same time, while the majority of Canadians exhibited that spirit there were here and there some people making the war an opportunity for self-aggrandizement. There were grafters in the sale of surgical supplies, grafters in the sale of horses, grafters in the sale of potatoes, all of which did not redound to the honour of Canada. That is one thing we do not wish to take place concerning the expenditures of these money's, if it can possibly be avoided. I know that such conditions almost inevitably creep in, and my appeal to the people of Canada would be to exercise something of the spirit of cooperation and self-sacrifice they manifested during the war.
I shall now say something I had not intended to say, but which is prompted by what happened in the house this evening. The hon-member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) made certain charges regarding the expenditure of part of the S20,000,000. Whether or not those charges were true I do not know, but I must say I noted with regret that when the hon. member was making them many hon. members opposite seemed' to treat his remarks with great levity, and as if there were no seriousness in them. It was with very great regret I noticed the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. McDade) stand in his place and attempt to belittle the remarks of the hon. member for Gloucester. I believe the time will come when the hon. member opposite (Mr. McDade) will have the grace to be ashamed of that portion of his speech, and will widh it to be expunged from the record.
In making a plea for cooperation among the people of Canada the point that has been in. my mind during the past few weeks has been the necessity for cooperation on the part of those who are in need of relief, whether it be direct or through the furnishing of employment. I wish particularly to appeal to labour members in the house who, I am sorry to say, I do not see iij their seats. The hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) and Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) have frequently emphasized the necessity for high wages. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that it is not desirable that this money Should be spent in the spirit of trying to keep men down to a bare living wage. I do not think the people of Canada would wish that men should be

Farm and Unemployment Relief
paid a mere pittance for a fair day's work. At tlhe same time, however, it would be well for those who undertake to represent labour in this house to impress upon their constituents the necessity of giving the heartiest kind of cooperation to the people of Canada in this great emergency. It may be that the great majority of their constituents are willing to do so, but we do know that unfortunately there are large numbers of people who would not be willing to cooperate.
Perhaps the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been an employer of labour, and because of that would be able to view the matter of employment from both sides. I hope that at some time in his life the hon. member has had that experience. Some of us have worked as labouring men, and have afterwards been employers of labour. We are in a position to view labour matters from both angles because we have lived and worked on both sides. My own opinion would be that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has very seldom, if ever, been an employer of labour and for that reason he may not be able to view labour matters from the standpoint of having to pay a very unsatisfactory labourer the high wage he might demand.
I shall give an illustration. Last harvest time we in the prairies provinces recognized that owing to prevailing conditions we would not be in a position to pay the wages we had formerly paid to labourers at that time of the year. When prices were good we did not begrudge paying high wages, but it was not an uncommon thing last harvest time for men who were offered wages we were able to pay, to say, "Oh, it is no concern of ours that the price of wheat has gone down; that is nothing to us. We want certain wages." Just so far as that spirit prevails, just that far will our whole efforts to relieve present difficulties meet with failure. My plea to Canadian people in all walks of life would be to exercise that spirit of self-sacrifice and cooperation which was shown during the war and as far as possible let their actions be free from the graft which took place during the war and which brought nothing but dishonour to the fair name of Canada.
We are passing through a difficult time. I know there is no doubt in this house as to the necessity for relief measures. With a proper spirit of cooperation among all classes of the people I believe we will weather this emergency, severe though it be.

subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext:
The resolution before the house, Mr. Speaker, is a frank recognition by society of its obligation towards its less fortunate members. Per-

haps it is unnecessary now to discuss the situation in Saskatchewan, but I might say that in a speech delivered recently by the premier of that province he stated that there were 160,000 people living in districts in which there was no crop whatever. There are also many thousands of others in districts where there is very little crop and these also will need some assistance.
In a number of articles in the Winnipeg Tribune, written by the editor of that journal, Mr. McTavish, which articles were reproduced in the Ottawa Citizen, he points out a rather interesting thing. He noticed that the people in the districts in which there was no crop whatever seemed to be taking it quite philosophically and had ceased to worry. They knew they were safe from the bailiff, from the mortgage companies and from the banks, that nobody was going to interfere with them or try to dispossess them of their homes or their stock as long as they had no crop whatever, and they knew also that in the last analysis the government would see that they were provided with feed for their stock and the necessaries of life for another year. But he pointed out that strangely enough when he went to another part of the country where the crops were fair he found the people were worried because they knew they had to rely on their own resources, they did not expect the government to look after them, and the mortgage companies and other creditors would be expecting to get something out of the crop in reduction of their claim. That is one of the anomalies of the situation. Where there is a fair crop-and there is in my constituency -the farmers are in distress because that crop will be taken off probably at a loss; at any rate it will mean no profit whatever. My point is that the distress will not be entirely confined to the districts where there is no crop.
Now, we have a tremendous trek of population from the dry districts to the districts in the north, the bush districts, where at least there is grass and water and something growing. Hundreds of people from the southern parts of the province have come into my district, and in dealing with this trek, which is something unprecedented in that country, I might quote, in part, an editorial in a recent issue of The Western Producer. It says:
Another evidence of the condition in western Canada is the increasing abandonment of farms by harassed agriculturists. During the past month or two there was to be seen any day the spectacle of a family moving northward with what is left of its meagre possessions. A thousand tragedies are slowly moving north on the dusty roads: a man, a woman, two or three

Farm and Unemployment Relief
children, a few skinny horses, a decrepit cow or two, some sticks of furniture, a few worried hens; moving north, in search of water, in search of food, in search of the means to sustain life.
These people are now in the north, many of them in my constituency, many of them I understand in the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir). While they have moved in there on to bush homesteads too late to produce any crop, while they may have grass and feed and water for their animals, yet they will have to be provided with the means of sustaining life through the winter and of putting in a crop in the spring.
I was glad to hear what the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) said about the necessity of providing work rather than giving charity. I think we can all agree that that is the best way to look after needy people-to give them the means of earning something rather than a direct charitable hand^out. In that country we need roads very very badly. One may travel hundreds of miles on roads that are barely passable after a heavy rain. The province would no doubt contribute its quota towards their construction, and I think that with some cooperation between the two governments roads can be built and work provided for needy farmers at the same time.
There is a great deal, too, in what the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) said. In prosperous times when interest rates are high and commodities and materials are high in price, we seem to build our roads, erect our buildings and1 construct railway branch lines and other public works. Then when there is depression, when interest rates are low, when money can be borrowed very easily, when lumber and all other materials are low in price, we sit quietly by waiting for prosperity to come. I do believe that the government has a direct responsibility to do what it can in such periods of depression. The money spent in a period of prosperity means a double debt when we come to a period of depression. The money we borrowed in 1928 and 1929, that is the actual debt, has doubled today; whereas if we spent money now, in a couple of years when we hope there will be a period of prosperity, when we hope commodity prices, wages and so on will be high again, we would find it very much easier to pay the debt so incurred than if we deferred the expenditure to that time. So I do think it is good business on the part of the government to engage in all the public works they can at the present time. In so far as a good deal of the province of Saskatchewan is concerned, I feel that the best means of providing
relief would be to do some necessary roadwork in cooperation with the province. The situation is so serious that the government should place the whole resources of the country behind the effort to deal with unemployment and with agricultural distress.
Now, there has been a lot of discussion across the floor because the Prime Minister, it is objected, is asking parliament to give him a blank cheque for the amount of money to be spent. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) objected very strongly to that and, if I caught him rightly, he used these words: "We will give him"-referring to the Prime Minister-"anything he asks if he will only name the amount." Now, I do not see very much difference between that and giving the Prime Minister a blank cheque. The Prime Minister in effect says: "Give me a blank cheque and I will not spend any more than is absolutely necessary." The leader of the opposition retorts: "If you will just say the amount, regardless of what that amount is, I will support you." So in effect the leader of the opposition is prepared to give the Prime Minister a blank cheque; that is what he is offering to do. In any case I do not see that it makes very much difference. We talk about the rights of parliament, but how much does it mean after all? In the last analysis the expenditure of money is controlled by the government. The government has a majority in the house and can always force those expenditures through. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) seems to be shocked because the hon. member for Wetaskiwin subscribed to this principle in the resolution. I am sorry the hon. member is not in his seat, but I would say to him that as a private member he has never had any control over expenditures. He can get up and protest against any expenditure, as he did to-night, but the estimate or the bill goes through because the government has a majority. So I do not see any particular difference so far as that is concerned.
I am not altogether clear as to what is involved in the measures that are proposed to be taken to maintain law and order. That is something we do not like to think about at a time like this. 1 think we all agree that the first duty of a government is to maintain law and order. Every member of the house will subscribe to that principle, but I do hope nothing very drastic will be undertaken by the government in that regard.
The Prime Minister spoke rather severely about certain agitators in the country who should be dealt with, and with whom the government intended to deal rather severely-

Farm and Unemployment Relief
I think often we take these men too seriously; in fact we dignify them and enhance their importance by taking them seriously. The ordinary soap box orator, with the little group around him, is only as serious and as dangerous as we take him to be. In discussing this question the late President Wilson said:	"I tell you the so-called
radicalism of our day is simply nature's way of relieving the generous energies of our people." So I would say to the government that if they are faced with any threats of disorder they should fight that threat with bread rather than with bullets. Bread is always much more effective in times of distress, and when hungry men get riotous bread is always a much more effective weapon than bullets. I trust that is the weapon upon which the government will rely.
As a last word I would ask the Prime Minister to look seriously into this question of providing relief in Saskatchewan by having necessary road work done in order to give employment to needy farmers.

subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext:
I desire to make a few remarks in connection with the very important resolution now under discussion. First of all I must say this measure will have a wonderful reception in that part of the country I have the honour to represent, because of certain local conditions we must face immediately. I believe we fully understand now that this matter of unemployment is of national importance; for that reason alone we will have a central organization and the old hit-and-miss policy under which we proceeded last winter will be done away with. That will be doing something tangible in a national way.
One of the details I have in mind is the way wages were paid the workingmen under the unemployment relief fund last winter. I have in my hand a statement made by Senator Robertson as reported in the Toronto Mail and Empire of February 7, 1931, in which he stated that the Ontario government and the federal government cooperated in the expenditure of over $2,000,000 in the construction of rural roads in northern Ontario. The quotation is as follows:
The federal and provincial authorities agreed that it would be wise that the opportunity to secure work should be spread to as many needy people as possible. It was therefore decided that the men should work eight-hour days instead of the customary ten hours. We felt that 25 to 30 cents an hour was not enough, particularly with men working only eight hours and we fixed 35 cents as the minimum in all road work in which the Dominion government cooperates. The men working in northern

Ontario are getting from 5 to 10 cents an hour more than was the scale before unemployment relief was inaugurated by the Dominion government and are working two hours a day less.
I believe the Minister of Labour was sincere in making that statement, but I am sorry to say that principle was not applied in the section of the country from which I come; it was not applied to the ridings of North Timiskaming, South Timiskaming or Nipissing. During the progress of a recent provincial by-election in Hamilton I was amazed to learn that a minister of the Ontario government stated that in the Fort William-Port Arthur and Kenora districts the men doing road work under the employment relief fund received $2.80 for an eight hour day. In my section of the country they were paid only at the rate of $2.40 for an eight hour day. I believe the same rate should have applied in my section of the country; we are part and parcel of northern Ontario and the cost of living is just as high there as it is in other sections of the north. So I ask the government to go into this matter and if possible pay to the settlers and the workingmen who did that road work last winter that difference of 40 cents a day.
Hon. gentlemen must realize that 40 cents per day means a great deal to a man who has been out of work for weeks or 'perhaps months. Hon. Mr. Finlayson said, only a few days ago, that this anomaly would be remedied in a very simple manner, that the government were going to lower the wages of men working on the roads in northern Ontario to $2.40 per day. This is not playing fair with the north. The men should be paid at least the wage promised by the Minister of Labour last winter when he was speaking in Toronto. We expected, and had the right to expect, that the settlers and workingmen of our section of the country would receive that wage. Very strong protests have appeared in the press of northern Ontario. The Porcupine Advance, a Conservative paper, made an urgent appeal to the provincial government making it plain that they were not playing fair; the Northland Post of Cochrane, an independent paper, and the Kapuskasing Tribune both took the same stand.
I appeal to the Prime Minister to see that this situation is remedied as soon as possible. Hon. gentlemen will readily see the importance of this matter in our section of the country where most of the men were allowed to work only three days per week at $2.40 per day, making a total of $7.20 per week. We must remember the climatic conditions which exist in that part of the country, and I may tell the house that during most of the winter the average time spent on road work did not ex-

Questions
ceed 20 days per month. It will be seen that for the father of a family or a settler trying to hew a living out of a new section of the country it was absolutely impossible to make ends meet. Again I ask that the difference be paid to every man who worked on the roads last winter in my section of the country; they should be paid the wage which was paid in other sections of northern Ontario.
There is one other protest I desire to make. I believe that in centralizing the control of the expenditure of the money for unemployment relief single men should be given a fair chance in the north. Perhaps I am treading on dangerous ground when I discuss this question, but it must be realized that in the newer sections of the country, whether they be in northern Ontario, northern Quebec or the western provinces, many single men have settled from the older sections of Canada. They have tried to start farms, and it is not their fault that they are single, because in many instances they intend to marry when they are in a position to do so. Last winter in my section of the country we had the sad spectacle of poor single men who had been working on farms for many years absolutely refused work, with no inquiry made as to their circumstances. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that this is not playing the game with a very good section of the population of northern Ontario.
I would direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that it is now eleven o'clock.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, July 30, 1931.
